contributing/contributing.title: 🛠️ Contributing
contributing/contributing.text: 🛠️ Contributing How the engine's code is laid out, how to build and test it, and how a change is proposed. Read the style guide next: it says how the code is written. The code The repository is one Go module. Its packages are divided by meaning, and depend one way: the game's library never imports the editor's. Package What it holds space Vectors, rotations, transforms and boxes: the maths, in metres animation Tweens physics The 2D physics: bodies, gravity, zones, platforms scenefile The files: scenes, sprites, tilesets, read, written and checked shapes The shapes' meshes failure Error codes engine The running game: nodes, scenes, behaviours, input, drawing, Run project A project's folder: create, import, build, its behaviours read from its code editor The editor, which a game installs in itself while it is made cmd/go-engine The go-engine command: new , open, -update internal/build Building for each platform, and finding its tools internal/install Installing the tools from the editor internal/notices The licences a built game carries internal/style Tests of the style guide's rules a program can check examples/platformer The quest's game, a module of its own What a game imports ( engine , space , animation , physics , scenefile , shapes ) builds with TinyGo for the 3DS: no cgo, and no files read from a disk. Drawing, windows and input go through Go Renderer and Go UI ; what they lack is added there, not here. Build and test go vet ./... go test ./... # no display needed go run ./cmd/go-engine new /tmp/try "Try" # a project to try changes on go run ./cmd/go-engine /tmp/try # the editor: a display and OpenGL 4.1 go run ./cmd/go-engine -capture shot.png /tmp/try # one frame of the editor to a picture -capture takes the editor's flags too: -select Node , -play , -workspace build , -3ds , -dark , -width and -height . The pictures in these pages were made with it. After changing a public name or an error code, write the reference again: python3 docs/6-reference/generate.py Proposing a change A small fix is a change, a test and a commit. Anything larger goes through a proposal , one file in proposals : why, what (each requirement with a check), what is out of scope, the design, the tasks, and at the end the result. The author approves the proposal, then the plan, before anything is built. The proposals there are the record of why the engine is the way it is. Every change in behaviour comes with its test, and its docs in the same commit. Work goes on a feature/… branch; main holds what the author has reviewed. Commits area: what changed , in the imperative: physics: carry what stands on a platform . Commits written with an AI assistant end with a Co-Authored-By: line naming it. ← Troubleshooting · Style guide →

contributing/style-guide.title: 📐 Style guide
contributing/style-guide.text: 📐 Style guide go-engine's code must be easy to follow for a junior developer, or for anyone who can read code. These rules hold everywhere in the repository, and in the code the editor writes into new projects. A test ( internal/style ) checks the ones a program can check. 1. English, always Code, comments, names, error codes, commit messages and documentation are in English. 2. Names say what things are Whole words. No acronyms and no abbreviations: position , not pos ; index , not i ; context , not ctx ; message , not msg ; button , not btn . Exceptions , because they are what everyone calls them: | Name | Why | |---|---| | err | the error a call returned, as all Go code names it | | x , y , z | the axes' own names, for a coordinate | | ui | the name of the go-ui package when it is imported | | init | the function Go itself runs when a package loads; no other name works | Short English words are words , not abbreviations: at , by , to , up , is are fine. Tests call their *testing.T test , not t . No mathematical shorthand a junior would have to look up: Vector , not Vec3 ; Rotation , not Quat ; Toward , not Lerp . Say the unit when there is one: seconds , pixelsPerMetre , degrees . Booleans read as a question: visible , isCamera , found , playing . Functions are verbs, or what they give back: LoadScene , Bounds , MainCamera . Don't repeat the package: space.Transform , not space.SpaceTransform . // No func upd(n *Node, dt float64) { n.T.Pos.X += n.V * dt } // Yes func moveForward(node *Node, seconds float64) { node.Transform.Position.X += node.Speed * seconds } 3. One function, one job A function does one thing , and its name says which. If a function needs a comment to split it into parts, split it into functions instead. As a guide, a function fits on a screen: about 40 lines at most . A longer one is usually doing two jobs. A function that finds something does not also change it. // No: reads, checks and builds in one place func Load(files fs.FS, file string) (*Scene, error) { /* 80 lines */ } // Yes: each step has a name func Load(files fs.FS, file string) (*Scene, error) { data, err := fs.ReadFile(files, file) if err != nil { return nil, failure.Wrap(SceneNotFound, file, err) } description, err := scenefile.Read(data) if err != nil { return nil, failure.Wrap(SceneUnreadable, file, err) } return Build(files, description) } 4. Early returns Handle the errors and the special cases first, and return . The normal path then runs down the left margin, without else and without nesting. // No func (node *Node) Shape() string { if node != nil { if node.shape != "" { return node.shape } else { return "none" } } return "" } // Yes func (node *Node) Shape() string { if node == nil { return "" } if node.shape == "" { return "none" } return node.shape } 5. Errors have codes Every error go-engine returns carries a code from the failure package. A program checks the code, never the error's text. Each package declares its codes as variables, near the top of an errors.go file: // Error codes of the engine package. var ( SceneNotFound = failure.Define("engine.scene-not-found", "the scene file does not exist") SceneUnreadable = failure.Define("engine.scene-unreadable", "the scene file is not a scene") ) Names of codes: the package, a dot, and the error in a few words joined by dashes. Return the bare code when there is nothing to add: it costs nothing. Wrap when there is detail worth knowing (which file, which name, the error underneath): failure.Wrap(SceneNotFound, file, err) . Check with failure.Is(err, engine.SceneNotFound) (or errors.Is , which does the same). Performance: a bare code is a pointer to a value made once, so returning it allocates nothing and comparing it compares two pointers. Wrap allocates once, so it belongs in loading, saving and building, never in a frame's update . Code that runs every frame does not make errors. 6. Packages and modules A package and a module divide different things: Package Module What it is A folder of Go code with a name ( space , engine ) A set of packages with a go.mod , versioned and published together What dividing is for Meaning : each concept in its place Publishing : things that change at different paces A unit of Compiling and importing Versions, releases and dependencies Dividing packages, by meaning A package is a concept you can name. Its name is a good prefix for what is in it: space.Vector , animation.Tween , scenefile.Node . If no such name fits, the boundary is wrong. The two-package test. If using one almost always means importing the other, they are one package. Distinct ideas apart, even small ones. A package of two files is fine if it is an idea of its own ( failure ). No util , common , helpers , misc , api , types . They mean nothing, and gather dependencies. Dependencies point one way. The basic concepts know nothing of the ones built on them: failure, space the base: they import nothing of ours ↑ animation, scenefile, shapes, physics ↑ engine what a game carries; builds for the 3DS ↑ project desktop tools ↑ editor → cmd/go-engine When something below needs something above ( engine importing editor ), the concept is in the wrong package. The editor's hook is the other way round for this reason: the editor registers itself with the engine, which never imports it. What a game carries stays portable. The packages a game imports build with TinyGo for the 3DS: no editor, no go/parser , no os/exec in them. What a package imports decides what goes into a .3dsx . What only go-engine uses goes in internal/ . It can change without breaking anyone's game. Inside a package, divide into files, not into more packages: node.go , scene.go , errors.go , each a part of the concept. Package names follow Go's: lower case, one word (two words written together when needed, as filepath or scenefile ), short and clear, with no abbreviation (our rule goes further than Go's, which allows familiar ones as fmt ), not the name of a common variable, and not repeated in what the package holds ( http.Server , not http.HTTPServer ). Dividing modules, by publishing Go's advice is one repository, one module , unless there is a strong reason: "For all but power users, you probably want to adopt the usual convention that one repo = one module" (Russ Cox, in Go's modules FAQ). More modules cost work: go test ./... no longer tests everything, replace directives must be kept between them, and adding, removing or versioning one takes care. A part becomes a module of its own when: it is published and versioned apart , used by other projects at their own pace; it has very different or heavy dependencies that those who use only the other part should not have to take; different people look after it. Not for size alone: Go downloads through its module proxy, and a program only links the packages it imports, whatever module they are in. Applied to the author's libraries: go-renderer, go-ui, go-sound, tinygo-3ds and go-engine are separate modules because each is published and reused on its own (go-ui serves without go-engine, go-sound without go-renderer). go-engine stays one module : a game for the 3DS links engine and what it imports, never editor , so splitting would add replace directives and versions to keep in step for nothing. That would change if another project wanted only space and animation without go-ui and GLFW, or if the editor came to be released at a pace of its own. The packages today Package Concept Who uses it failure Error codes Every package space Positions, rotations, transforms, boxes Games and the engine animation Values that move over time Games scenefile The scene file format The engine and the editor shapes Meshes of simple shapes The engine physics 2D boxes that fall, collide and slide The engine engine The running game: nodes, behaviours, input, cameras Games project A game's folder: creating, building, reading its code The editor (desktop only) editor The editor's window The game while it is being made (desktop only) internal/build Running Go and TinyGo project internal/notices Third-party notices project internal/style The tests of this guide The repository Sources: Package names (the Go blog), Organizing a Go module (go.dev), Go modules FAQ: should I have multiple modules in a single repository? , and Google's Go style guide, best practices (package size, errors). 7. Comments A comment says why , or what a reader cannot see in the code. It does not repeat the code. Every exported name has a comment that starts with the name: // Bounds is the box… . A package starts with a comment saying what it is for, with an example when it helps. 8. Files A file holds one part of its package: node.go , scene.go , errors.go . No file of thousands of lines, and no swarm of tiny files either. 9. Tests Every change comes with tests, and go vet ./... and go test ./... pass before a commit. A test's name is a sentence about what must be true: TestAChildIsPlacedInsideItsParent . 10. Performance in a frame What runs every frame (a behaviour's Update , drawing, input) must not allocate when it can avoid it: reuse slices and lists, keep texts that do not change, and make no errors. See 3ds.md in go-ui for why it matters most on the console. ← Contributing

core-ideas.title: 💡 Core ideas

sections.text: A game is a Go module
The editor lives inside your game

core-ideas.text: 💡 Core ideas A handful of ideas explain how everything in Go Engine behaves. Read this page once, and the editor, the scene files and the code will rarely surprise you. A game is a Go module There is no special language and no project format to learn. A game is a folder with a go.mod , like any Go program. Its scenes and pictures are files in it, and main.go carries them inside the game (Go's embed ), so the finished program needs nothing beside it. Why a plain module? Because then everything Go already has works: your code editor finds the engine's functions and their comments, go test tests the game, and go build builds it. The editor lives inside your game go-engine does not run your code itself. It builds your game with the editor in it ( editor.go ) and starts that. So the editor knows your behaviours because they are compiled into it, and Play plays your real code, frame by frame, inside its view. The price is small: after changing the code, Rebuild (in Code) builds the game again and reopens the editor where you were. The editor only starts when go-engine asks for it: go run . plays the game. Builds for players leave the editor's code out altogether ( -tags release ), and so does the 3DS. Scenes are trees of nodes A scene is a file, scenes/*.scene.json , that the editor writes and you can read. It holds a tree of nodes , as a family tree holds people. A node is a thing in the scene, and what it is comes from its parts: Part Makes the node… a shape or a model something solid in 3D: a cube, a house from a .glb a sprite a picture in 2D, perhaps animated a tile map a 2D level painted with tiles a camera the eye the scene is seen through a body something the 2D physics moves or stops a light a lamp, or a glowing sign behaviours something your code moves Each node has a transform : where it is, how it is turned and how large it is, relative to its parent . Move a ship and its sailors move with it. node.World() says where a node is in the world. Behaviours are your code A behaviour is a Go type with methods the engine calls, each one optional, on a pointer: Method When Start(context *engine.Context) Once, before the scene's first frame Update(context *engine.Context) Every frame; context.Delta is the seconds since the last one Touched(context *engine.Context, other *engine.Node) When a moving body, other , begins touching the node's trigger The context holds the node the behaviour is on, the scene, Time (the seconds since the scene started) and the player's input. main.go registers each behaviour once, with an empty value of it, engine.Register(Spin{}, Player{}) , and the scene names it by its Go type's name, Spin . Its exported fields are its settings, filled from the scene by their JSON names, so one behaviour can drive many nodes, each set differently. // Bob moves its node up and down. type Bob struct { Height float64 `json:"height"` // metres } func (bob *Bob) Update(context *engine.Context) { context.Node.Transform.Position.Y = 0.5 + bob.Height*math.Sin(context.Time*3) } A behaviour finds another with engine.Behaviour[Player](node) , which gives the behaviour and whether the node has one. context.Find("Car/Wheel") finds a node by its path from the scene's top; node.Find("Wheel") from a node, among its children. context.ChangeScene(file) goes to another scene, and context.RestartScene() starts this one again. Everything is in metres Unit One unit is a metre, in 2D and 3D alike Axes Y up, X to the right, Z towards whoever looks (right-handed, as glTF , the format of 3D models) Forward A node with no turn faces -Z, as a camera does Turns Degrees: X tilts, Y turns, Z rolls; a positive turn is counter-clockwise, seen from the axis's positive end Scale Times the node's own size; shapes are a metre across The editor's grid has one-metre cells, darker every five; X is red, Y green and Z blue. 2D is 3D seen from the front Whether a scene is 2D or 3D is the scene's choice: New 2D scene , or the 3D | 2D switch over the view. A 2D scene uses the same metres, seen from the front by a camera without perspective, and shows sprites, tile maps and flat shapes (a cube is drawn as a square). A sprite is as large as its pixels at the scene's pixels per metre , set in the scene's inspector: at 32, a sprite 32 pixels high stands a metre high. Z only says what is drawn in front: the larger, the nearer. Isometric is 3D seen from a fixed angle, so the three axes look the same length. Physics moves bodies, in 2D A 2D node with a body is moved by the scene's physics while the game plays. Its kind says how: Kind What it does Solid Never moves; others stand on it and stop against it (ground, walls) Moving Falls, moves at the velocity its behaviours give it, stops against solids (the player) Pushable Falls; a moving body stands on it, or pushes it by walking into it (a box) Platform Never falls, moves through solids at its velocity, carrying what stands on it (a lift) Trigger Stops nothing; its behaviours hear what touches it (a coin, a door) A falling body has a gravity scale : 1 is Earth's pull, 2 twice as strong, 0 none. A trigger can have a gravity of its own, a pull : what falls inside it is pulled that way. "On the floor" is wherever a body's gravity pulls it, so a body pulled up stands on a ceiling. Light multiplies colours A scene can be lit. Its ambient is the light that reaches everything: white at 1 leaves the colours as they are, a dark blue at 0.4 is a night. Lights on nodes add to it where they shine, like lamps in a dark room, and can brighten up to twice. A scene with neither is drawn unlit, at no cost. A 3D scene always has a sun and a sky, which light it by day or night; its lights are lamps that shine on the shapes around them besides. Not yet Sound, and a game's own interface (menus, a score on screen). Bodies that turn, slopes, and shapes other than boxes. Textures from models: they are drawn with their colours. Moving and turning things with handles in the view (the inspector and dragging do it now). ← Get started · The quest →

getting-started.title: 🚀 Get started
getting-started.text: 🚀 Get started In fifteen minutes you install Go Engine, make a project, play its first scene in the editor and change what its code does. Nothing here needs a game idea yet. What you need Go 1.25 or newer ( go.dev/dl ). A C compiler : the editor's window speaks to the graphics card through C. On Linux, sudo apt install gcc libgl1-mesa-dev xorg-dev libwayland-dev libxkbcommon-dev (Debian, Ubuntu); on macOS, xcode-select --install ; on Windows, the gcc of MSYS2 (Windows is still to be tried). OpenGL 4.1 , which any computer of the last ten years has. 1. Install the editor go install github.com/akrck02/go-engine/cmd/go-engine@latest This puts a program called go-engine in Go's bin folder ( go env GOPATH , then bin ). If the shell cannot find it, add that folder to your PATH . 2. Make a project go-engine new ~/games/harbour "Harbour lights" The second word is the game's name, as players will see it. A project is a folder with a Go module inside; the command writes it, fetches the engine as go does any module, and opens the editor: File What it is engine.json The game's name and the scene it starts with scenes/main.scene.json The first scene: a ground, a cube and a camera main.go Carries the scenes and assets inside the game, and starts it spin.go A first behaviour: the code that turns the cube editor.go Puts the editor inside the game while you make it Checkpoint: the editor shows a coloured cube on a green ground. Next time, open the project with go-engine ~/games/harbour . On a computer with no screen (a server), go-engine new -open=false makes the project without opening the editor. 3. Look around The bar at the bottom changes between six workspaces , one job each. The keys 1 to 6 do it too. Workspace What it is for Project The project's files: pictures, models, scenes, and its settings Art Cutting a picture into frames for animations, or into tiles for levels Level Arranging a scene: the nodes on the left, the view, the inspector on the right Code The behaviours the project's Go code declares, and where they are used Play Playing the scene, with a pause, a step of one frame, and a log Build Making the game for a computer, the 3DS or an Android phone In Level , drag the view to turn round the scene, scroll to come closer, and click a thing in it to choose it. Each thing in a scene is a node : the ground, the cube and the camera are three, listed on the left. The chosen node's inspector on the right shows where it is, what it is, and its behaviours. 4. Play Press Play in the bar at the bottom (or 5): the scene starts playing at once, through its camera, and the cube turns. Play always plays the scene as it is now, saved or not. Checkpoint: the cube turns slowly. Stop (or Escape) goes back to the workspace you were in, with the scene as it was before playing. 5. Change a number Back in Level , choose the cube. Its inspector shows the Spin behaviour with a field, speed , at 45. Make it 180 and play again: the cube spins four times as fast. That field comes from the code. Open spin.go in your code editor: // Spin turns its node around the vertical axis. type Spin struct { Speed float64 `json:"speed"` // degrees a second } // Update runs every frame, with the seconds since the last one in context.Delta. func (spin *Spin) Update(context *engine.Context) { context.Node.Transform.Turn(space.Up, spin.Speed*context.Delta) } Every exported field of a behaviour is a field in the inspector, named by its JSON name. Update runs every frame; context.Delta is the seconds since the last frame. main.go registers the behaviour, so scenes can name it: engine.Register(Spin{}) 6. Change the code Make the cube bob up and down as it turns. Add a field and two lines to spin.go : import ( "math" "github.com/akrck02/go-engine/engine" "github.com/akrck02/go-engine/space" ) type Spin struct { Speed float64 `json:"speed"` // degrees a second Bob float64 `json:"bob"` // metres up and down } func (spin *Spin) Update(context *engine.Context) { context.Node.Transform.Turn(space.Up, spin.Speed*context.Delta) context.Node.Transform.Position.Y = 0.5 + spin.Bob*math.Sin(context.Time*3) } context.Time is the seconds since the scene started. The editor runs inside your game, so it needs the game built again: open Code (or 4) and press Rebuild , which glows while the code is newer than the game. It saves the scene, builds, and reopens the editor where you were; if the code does not compile, the error shows under Output , and the editor stays as it was. Open in code editor opens the project in the editor engine.json names ( codeEditor ), or in $VISUAL . Checkpoint: the cube's inspector now has a bob field. Make it 0.5 and play: the cube bobs. 7. Play it on its own In Build (or 6), the card This computer has Build , which writes the game into the project's build/ folder, and Play , which opens it in a window of its own. From a terminal, go run . in the project's folder plays it too: the editor only starts when go-engine asks. The other cards make the game for the Nintendo 3DS and for Android phones. The tools they need are set up in Tools , the tab beside Platforms at the top of Build; the guides explain them. Where next 🗺️ The quest : make a whole platformer, a level at a time. 💡 Core ideas : what a scene, a node and a behaviour really are. ← Overview · Core ideas →

guides/a-2d-level-with-tiles.title: 🧱 A 2D level with tiles
guides/a-2d-level-with-tiles.text: 🧱 A 2D level with tiles Paint a level with a tileset, and let its solid tiles be the ground. For a first walk through it, see level 3 of the quest . The shortest way In Project , choose a picture of tiles and press Make it a sprite or a tileset , then A tileset . Set Pixels a tile, a side (16, 32…) and save. The tileset is a file beside the picture, name.tileset.json , that every scene shares. Still in Art , click the tiles bodies should stand on: they turn blue, solid. In Level , press + , Tile map , and choose the tileset in its inspector. Set how many cells across and down it has. Choose a tile in the palette under the view, and paint: B paints, E erases, G fills, V goes back to choosing nodes. Set the scene's pixels per metre to the tile's size, so a tile is a metre. How it behaves Where The map's top-left corner is its node's position; a cell is a tile's pixels at the scene's pixels per metre Solid tiles Each run of solid tiles side by side becomes one solid box while the game plays: the ground, walls and ceilings Depth The map is drawn at its node's draw order, like any 2D node Several maps A scene can have many: a background one with no solid tiles, a foreground one to stand on Variations A bare picture as tiles. A tile map can name a picture instead of a tileset. Its inspector then asks for the tile size, and the palette has Bodies stand on tile … to choose solid ones. A tileset is better as soon as two scenes share the tiles. Bigger or smaller maps. Changing the cells across and down keeps what is painted from the top-left corner, and empties the rest. A camera inside the level. A camera that follows keeps its view inside the tile maps: see A camera that follows . ← Guides · Sprites and animations →

guides/a-camera-that-follows.title: 🎥 A camera that follows
guides/a-camera-that-follows.text: 🎥 A camera that follows Make a 2D camera follow the player, smoothly, without showing past the level's edges. The shortest way Choose the Camera . Under Follows , choose the node to follow ( Player ), and set how many seconds it takes to catch up: 0 stays right on it, 0.2 feels smooth. That is all. What it sees Setting What it means Metres seen, top to bottom How much of the world fits on the screen's height Metres seen across, at least A width it never shows less of: on a phone held upright, the camera sees more height instead of losing the sides The scene is seen through this camera The main camera; a scene with several plays through this one Keeping inside the level Its view keeps inside chooses the limits: The tile maps (the default): the camera stops where the tiles end, at the sides and the bottom. The sky stays open, so it rises with a jump. Tick The top of the tile maps is a ceiling for a cave. A box of its own : four numbers, the lowest and highest X and Y it may show. Camera bounds , over the view, draws the box a following camera keeps its view in. Variations Following a moving platform. Follow the platform's node instead: anything can be followed. Look through it while editing. A camera's inspector has Look through it , to see the scene from it in the editor's view. ← Lights · Building for the 3DS →

guides/actions-and-controls.title: 🎮 Actions and controls

sections.text: Give them buttons in the editor

guides/actions-and-controls.text: 🎮 Actions and controls This guide is for whoever makes a game that plays on several devices. At the end you will read what the player does by name, give it buttons on each device in the editor, and design the sticks and buttons a phone shows. Read actions, not keys A game that reads Space works on a keyboard and nowhere else. A game that reads actions works anywhere: it asks for jump , and each device says which of its buttons jump. func (hero *Hero) Update(context *engine.Context) { if context.Input.Action("jump").Pressed { hero.Jump() } hero.Turn(context.Input.Action("turn").Value) // from -1 to 1 } An action presses ( Down , Pressed , Released ) or moves an axis ( Value , from -1 to 1). Give them buttons in the editor Open the Controls workspace. The actions are cards on the left, each in its own colour; the device is drawn in the middle, chosen in its tabs: Gamepad , Keyboard and mouse , Nintendo 3DS and Mobile . A pad and a keyboard play the same game on a computer and in a browser, so what you give them holds for both. Click a control of the device: a panel opens beside it. Pick an action, or type a new name and create it there. A button presses; a stick has two axes, across and up and down, each with its own action. The cards say which controls do each action; click one to see its controls stand out. The pencil renames it, the next icon switches it between pressing and an axis. Every change is kept in engine.json at once. Ctrl+Z undoes the last one. Design a phone's controls A phone has no buttons of its own, so the game draws them. Until you design some, it shows the engine's four: the arrows, B and A. In Mobile → Layout : Design the game's own starts from a stick and two buttons. Stick and Button add more; drag each where the thumbs rest. With one chosen, rename it, make it smaller or bigger, or remove it. Back in Actions , the controls on the screen get their actions like any other. Places and sizes are shares of the screen, so the layout fits every phone. ← The second screen · The reference →

guides/bodies-and-physics.title: 🪨 Bodies and physics
guides/bodies-and-physics.text: 🪨 Bodies and physics Make 2D nodes fall, stand, push and carry each other, and move them from code. Give a node a body Choose the node, and under Body press Give it a body . Choose its kind: Kind Use it for Solid Ground and walls: it never moves Moving The player and enemies: falls, moves at its velocity, stops against solids Pushable Boxes: falls, can be stood on, and is pushed when walked into Platform Lifts: moves as its behaviours say, carrying what stands on it Trigger Coins, doors, water: stops nothing, hears what touches it Its size is in metres; 0 is the node's own picture or shape. Moving and pushable bodies have a gravity scale: 1 is Earth's, more falls faster, 0 floats. Move it from code func (hero *Hero) Update(context *engine.Context) { body, found := context.Node.Body() if !found { return } body.Velocity.X = context.Input.Move().X * 4 // metres a second if context.Input.Pressed(engine.KeySpace) && body.OnFloor() { body.Velocity.Y = 12 } } Set the velocity ; never move a body's node by hand while it plays, or the physics loses it. OnFloor() tells whether the body stands on something. Hear what touches a trigger func (door *Door) Touched(context *engine.Context, other *engine.Node) { if _, isPlayer := engine.Behaviour[Player](other); isPlayer { context.ChangeScene("scenes/house.scene.json") } } Moving and pushable bodies touch triggers; Touched runs once, when the touch begins. Gravity zones A trigger can pull with a gravity of its own: tick A gravity of its own, for what falls inside and set the pull across and up, in metres a second each second (the world's is 0, -9.81). A field that lifts things is a pull upwards. A body that should keep the world's gravity anyway (the player walking through a field meant for boxes) ticks Keeps the world's gravity inside zones . "On the floor" follows the pull: a body pulled up stands on a ceiling. Variations The world's gravity. context.Scene.Physics().SetGravity(…) changes it for the whole scene. Tiles as ground. Solid tiles of a tile map are solid bodies already: see A 2D level with tiles . A lift. A platform with a behaviour that turns its velocity round at the top and bottom: the final challenge of the quest . ← Sprites and animations · Lights →

guides/building-for-android.title: 📱 Building for Android
guides/building-for-android.text: 📱 Building for Android Turn a game into an .apk , and play it on a phone or an emulator with its log in the editor. The tools In Build → Tools , press Install beside: Tool What it is for Android SDK Building and installing: Google's command-line tools, platform-tools, build-tools and a platform. Its licence is shown first, to read and accept Android NDK The C compiler for phones; it comes with the SDK JDK Java 17 or newer, which Android's tools need Android Studio's SDK and JDK are found too, if it is installed. Build and play On the Android card: Button What it does Build Writes build/<name>.apk , signed for trying Play on device Builds, installs on the phone or emulator adb sees, starts the game, and shows its log until it ends A phone needs USB debugging on (in its developer options) and a cable, or an emulator started. How the game behaves there Touch buttons. The game draws round buttons for the arrows, B and A; a keyboard plugged in still works. To place sticks and buttons of the game's own, design them in Controls → Mobile → Layout ( actions and controls ). TalkBack. With a screen reader on, the engine's buttons are read as Left , Right , B and A . A double tap presses one for a moment; a double tap held holds it, as a finger does. A game's own touch controls are not read yet. Held upright or sideways. Sideways, the game fills the screen. Upright, it sits at the top at its camera's shape, with the buttons under it. A camera's metres seen across keeps the level's sides in view. The application id. Android names apps by an id, as io.example.forest ; set it in Project → Settings . ← Building for the 3DS · The second screen →

guides/building-for-the-3ds.title: 🎮 Building for the 3DS
guides/building-for-the-3ds.text: 🎮 Building for the 3DS Turn a game into a .3dsx for the Nintendo 3DS's Homebrew Launcher, try it in an emulator, and send it to a console over Wi-Fi. The tools Open Build , then its Tools tab, and press Install beside each: Tool What it is for TinyGo Builds Go for the 3DS's processor: TinyGo for the 3DS 's release devkitPro Packs the program for the Homebrew Launcher, and sends it with 3dslink ; its installer runs in a terminal and asks for your password 3DS emulator Azahar, to try the game without a console Each tool can also be set by hand: type its place, or Browse , then Check . The places are kept for every project in go-engine/tools.json of your configuration folder. Build and play On the Nintendo 3DS card: Button What it does Build Writes build/<name>.3dsx , without the editor, with the notices of the code it carries Emulator Builds, and opens the game in the emulator Send Builds, and sends the game to a console: open the Homebrew Launcher there and press Y first Log What building said The console's address is found on the network; if it is not, set it in Project → Settings . How the game behaves there Screens The game is drawn on the top screen, 400 × 240; the bottom screen is free (see the second screen ) Buttons The cross and the circle pad are the arrows ( Input.Move() ), A is Space, B is Escape, X and Y their keys Speed 60 frames a second is the aim: lights, tiles and dozens of sprites keep it in the emulator Files The scenes and assets are inside the .3dsx ; the SD card is not read Variations Without the editor. In a terminal, in the project's folder: tinygo build -target=nintendo3ds -o game.3dsx . does what Build does, given TinyGo for the 3DS and devkitPro. ← A camera that follows · Building for Android →

guides/lights.title: 💡 Lights
guides/lights.text: 💡 Lights Light a scene, in 2D or 3D: an ambient for everything, lamps where they shine, and in 2D, pictures that glow. To see it done step by step, follow level 5 of the quest . A lamp Press + and choose Light , or choose any node and press Make it a light in its inspector. A point light shines all around its node: full within its inner radius, fading to nothing at its outer one, in metres. Its intensity is how strong it is: 1 a plain lamp, up to 2. It moves with its node, and grows with its scale. The ambient Choose nothing, and in the scene's inspector tick An ambient light of its own : 2D 3D What it is The light that reaches everything, in a colour and an intensity How strong the sky's light is None Daylight when the scene has lights, no lighting at all when it has none The sky lights as it is White at 1 leaves the colours as they are; a dark blue at 0.4 is a night. A picture that glows (2D) A sprite light shines through its node's picture, in its place, and the picture itself is not drawn: a window, a sign, a coin's gleam. Put it on a child of the node it lights, with the same sprite, so the node keeps its picture and gains the glow. In the editor Lights , over the 2D view, draws each light's two circles; in 3D, a chosen lamp shows two rings. Lit , over the 2D view, shows the scene lit as the game will be, or its colours unlit. From code A behaviour can change a light while the game plays: func (alarm *Alarm) Update(context *engine.Context) { light, found := context.Node.Light() if !found { return } alarm.strength = 1 + math.Sin(context.Time*6) // a field of Alarm: the light keeps pointing at it light.Intensity = &alarm.strength } How much it costs Lights cost nothing in a scene that has none. In 2D, all of a frame's lights are drawn into one picture at half the screen's resolution, then laid over the scene, so many lights cost little. In 3D, each thing drawn takes the four nearest lamps that reach it. On the 3DS, 3D lamps light at the vertices: a floor shows a lamp's pool only where it has vertices. ← Bodies and physics · A camera that follows →

guides/sprites-and-animations.title: 🎞️ Sprites and animations
guides/sprites-and-animations.text: 🎞️ Sprites and animations Show a picture in a 2D scene, cut a sheet into frames, and play its animations from code. A picture In Project , choose a picture (PNG or JPEG) and press Place in the scene . It is as large as its pixels at the scene's pixels per metre , times the node's scale. An animated sprite Choose the sheet's picture and press Make it a sprite or a tileset , then A sprite . In Art , set the frames across and down : a sheet of 4 frames in a row is 4 by 1. Under Animations , press Add , name it ( walk ), and click its frames on the picture, in order. Set its frames a second, and whether it Loops . Play it when the scene starts makes it the one a node starts with. Save. The sprite is a file, name.sprite.json , that every scene shares. Place it like a picture. From code func (hero *Hero) Update(context *engine.Context) { if context.Input.Move().X != 0 { context.Node.Play("walk") // keeps playing if it already is } else { context.Node.Play("idle") } context.Node.FaceLeft(context.Input.Move().X < 0) // mirrors the picture } Call What it does node.Play(name) Plays an animation of the node's sprite, from its start unless it is already playing; false if there is none of that name node.FaceLeft(left) Draws the picture mirrored, or not Variations A costume on a body. Put the sprite on a child of the node with the body, so it can sit a little higher or lower than the body's box (see level 2 of the quest ). Nodes that start differently. A node's inspector chooses the animation it starts with; nodes sharing one sprite file can each start on another. Pixel art stays sharp. Sprites are drawn at the nearest pixel, never blurred. ← A 2D level with tiles · Bodies and physics →

guides/the-second-screen.title: 🕹️ The second screen
guides/the-second-screen.text: 🕹️ The second screen Use a device's second screen (the 3DS's bottom one): a ready-made menu of the game's scenes, a screen drawn by the game itself, or a 3D scene of its own under it. A menu of the scenes In Project → Settings , tick List the scenes in the game's interface, to play any . The second screen then lists every scene; a touch plays it. It is handy while making a game, to jump to any level. A screen of your own engine.SetInterface draws the game's interface with Go UI , in the game's own look: on the second screen of a device that has one, over the window elsewhere. Call it in main.go , before engine.Run : func main() { engine.Register(Player{}) engine.SetInterface(levels) if err := engine.Run(files); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } // levels lists the levels, the one playing chosen; a touch plays another. func levels(context *ui.Context, menu engine.Menu) { for _, scene := range menu.Scenes() { playing := menu.Playing() != nil && menu.Playing().Name == scene.Name if context.Selectable("map", scene.Name, playing) { menu.Play(scene.File) } } } Call What it gives menu.Scenes() The project's scenes, each with its file and name menu.Playing() The scene playing, or nil menu.Play(file) Plays another scene It needs import ui "github.com/akrck02/go-ui" , which the engine already brings. The function runs every frame the interface is drawn. On the 3DS it fills the second screen, 320 × 240 pixels, where touch is its pointer; on a computer it is laid over the game's window. Variations A map, a score, the controls. Anything Go UI draws can be there: text, pictures, buttons. A 3D scene under it. engine.SetSecondScreen(scene) plays a scene of its own on the second screen, seen from its main camera, with the interface over it: a map that turns, a model in a shop. Its own pictures. Read a picture once ( draw2d.DecodeImage ) and paint it with context.Paint ; the Io World game draws its menu of levels from its own bricks this way. ← Building for Android · Actions and controls →

overview.title: Welcome to Go Engine 👋
overview.text: Welcome to Go Engine 👋 🚧 Go Engine is in development. What these pages describe can change from one version to the next: names, scene files and the editor's layout included. Go Engine makes games in Go. You arrange a game's scenes in its editor, and you write what moves in them in Go. One game runs on a computer, on an Android phone and on a Nintendo 3DS. A game is an ordinary Go module. Its scenes are files the editor writes, and its code is plain Go, written in any editor you like (Zed, Neovim, Visual Studio Code, GoLand…). The engine's small standard library gives that code the scene's nodes, the player's buttons and the time. Is it for me? ✅ You write Go, or want to, and want to make a small game : 2D, 3D or isometric. ✅ You want it to run on a handheld console : the 3DS, through homebrew. ✅ You want to learn how a game engine works inside: every part is readable Go. ❌ You need a finished engine to ship a commercial game: this one is young and changes often. Where to start If you… Read Time want to try it Get started : install it and play a first scene 15 min want to understand how it thinks Core ideas : games, scenes, nodes, behaviours 15 min want to learn step by step 🗺️ The quest : a forest platformer in six levels 2 h want to do one thing The guides : tiles, sprites, physics, lights, the 3DS — are looking up a name The reference : every package, and the scene files — are stuck Troubleshooting : errors by their code — want to change the engine Contributing : the code's layout, tests, style — What it can do Scenes 2D, 3D and isometric; shapes, .glb models, sprites with animations, tile maps Physics 2D bodies: solid, moving, pushable, platforms, triggers and gravity zones Lights Point lights in 2D and 3D, sprite lights, an ambient light Code Behaviours: Go types with Start and Update , played inside the editor Platforms Computers (tried on Linux; macOS and Windows still to try), Android and the Nintendo 3DS, built from the editor Not yet: sound, a game's own interface (menus, scores on screen), bodies that turn or slopes, and textures from models. The list lives in Core ideas . How it is built Go Engine stands on the author's other libraries: Go Renderer draws, Go UI is the editor's window, and TinyGo for the 3DS builds for the console. Every design decision has a proposal in proposals . 🤖 AI disclosure I write most of my code by hand, so I want to be clear about this project: it was written by an AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic) under my direction. Every commit made this way carries a Co-Authored-By: Claude line. Status: pending thorough review. The code compiles and its tests pass, but I have not yet reviewed it line by line. Treat it as a working draft, not as code I vouch for. Get started →

proposals/2d-lights.title: 8. Lights, in 2D and 3D
proposals/2d-lights.text: 8. Lights, in 2D and 3D Status: done, pending the author's review and a check of Metal on a Mac · Author's approval: proposal ☑ plan ☑ (2026-10-19, "Con metal": with Metal) · go-renderer's part, on its own feature/lights branch, is pushed only with the author's say (its CLAUDE.md) Why io-world's start screen in Unity was lit: a global light at 72 % dimmed the whole scene; the lamp cast a warm circle ( #faffa0 , 3.5 metres); the logo, "Press start" and the snail glowed through their own pictures; two thin lights lined "Demo". Made again in Go Engine (proposal 7), it is flat: the engine draws 2D with no light at all. Light is what gives a factory its gloom and a lamp its warmth. Any 2D game will want it, on the desktop, on phones and on the 3DS. Unity draws 2D lights in a pass of their own. It paints the lights into a light picture, cleared to the global light, and then multiplies the sprites by it. go-renderer's 2D drawing only paints one thing over another, with transparency. It has no way to add light, nor to multiply by it. What Id Requirement Check R1 go-renderer's 2D lists draw a light layer: lights added into a light picture cleared to an ambient colour, which then multiplies what the layer drew before it tests of draw2d 's commands; a test that renders a known list on OpenGL into pixels and compares R2 Three kinds of light: global (the ambient colour and intensity), point (a colour, intensity, inner and outer radius), sprite (a picture that glows as a light, tinted) tests per kind R3 The light layer draws on OpenGL (desktop), OpenGL ES (Android, the web), Metal (macOS) and the 3DS (citro3d) captures on each; the 3DS in Azahar; Metal by the author on a Mac R4 A 2D node can be a light ( light in scene files: kind, colour, intensity, radii); a scene's ambient light is the scene's own setting; lights move with their nodes tests in engine R5 Level shows and edits lights: an inspector for them, their radii drawn in the view, and the view lit as the game will be captures R6 Lights cost little: a 2D frame with lights allocates nothing, and on the 3DS a screen of eight lights keeps 60 frames a second the allocation test; a measure in Azahar and on the console R7 Io World's start screen has the Unity menu's seven lights, converted from MainMenu.unity by its script capture; the author on the console R8 (Added 2026-10-19, "debe funcionar en 2D y 3D".) A 3D node can be a point light too, with the same light (colour, intensity, radii) and the same fade as in 2D; a 3D scene's ambient scales its sky light tests in sceneplan and engine ; captures on OpenGL, GL ES and the 3DS R9 3D lights cost little: each draw takes at most four lights, the nearest that reach it, chosen once a frame on the processor for every backend; a frame allocates nothing for them tests of the choice; the allocation test R10 A lighting inside a clip lights only the clip, so a lit view inside the editor leaves the panels around it as they are a pixel test Out of scope Shadows cast by sprites or by 3D lights, normal maps, and spot lights (a later kind of the same light ). Dynamic lights on the 3DS's GPU (its fragment lighting). 3D lights are baked into vertex colours there, which suits lights that seldom move. Blend modes as a general tool for programs (only what the light layer needs). Design go-renderer ( draw2d , opengl , gles , ctr ), on feature/lights : draw2d : list.PointLight(x, y, inner, outer, colour) and list.SpriteLight(picture, area, colour) add lights. A colour's alpha is its intensity. list.Lighting(ambient) lights everything drawn before it with the lights since the last one, inside the clip it is made in. What comes after (an interface) stays unlit. (Built so instead of BeginLights/EndLights: one command marks where lighting happens, and nothing has to be closed.) OpenGL and GL ES: a light target the size of the screen, at half its resolution, since lights are soft. It is made like the backdrop's targets, and kept between frames. It is cleared to the ambient colour, and lights are drawn into it additively. A point light is one quad whose shader makes its falloff. Then it is drawn over the frame with a multiplying blend: one more draw call per light layer. 3DS ( ctr ): citro3d draws into a texture render target ( C3D_RenderTargetCreateFromTex ). It is at half the top screen's resolution, 256 by 128, since its sides must be powers of two. The PICA200 adds and multiplies with its own blend modes ( GPU_BLEND_ADD , GPU_DST_COLOR ). With no fragment shader on the 3DS, a point light's fade is read from a texture of sixteen discs. The ambient is painted in, since citro3d's clears run before a frame's draws. Metal: the same light target as a texture of its own, drawn with the same blends, written as the backdrop's Metal part was. It cannot be built nor run where this is written (Linux). The author checks it on a Mac. go-engine : scenefile : a node's light is {kind: point|sprite, colour, intensity, inner, outer} . A sprite light uses the node's own picture, and is drawn as a light instead of being shown. A scene's ambient colour and intensity is its global light. A scene with lights and no ambient is lit by daylight. (Changed while building: no "global" kind on nodes, since the scene's ambient is the global light. And no falloff setting: every backend fades with the same smooth curve.) engine : a 2D scene draws its sprites, then its lights (in their nodes' places and scales) into one light layer, then what goes above (the interface). Lights are found once a frame into a reused list, as the drawn nodes are. editor : a Light section in Level's inspector (kind, colour, intensity, radii). Radii are drawn as circles over the view when "Lights" is on, and Play is drawn lit. Io World : tools/make_start_screen.py reads the Unity menu's Light2D components into the start screen's nodes: type, colour, intensity, radii, and the sprite a sprite light uses. 3D (added with R8–R9). go-renderer's scene gets a list of point lights: position, linear colour times intensity, inner and outer radius. sceneplan chooses, for each draw, the four nearest lights whose outer sphere meets its bounds. It lists them by index, so every backend gets the same short list. (Built as "nearest", not "strongest": the simpler rule Godot's mobile renderer uses, and stable while nothing moves.) OpenGL and GL ES add them in their lit shading next to the sun. Each is Lambert light times the same smoothstep fade as 2D. They come from a fixed array of four uniforms: within OpenGL ES 2's uniform budget, and no light loop beyond four. The 3DS bakes them into its vertex colours with the sun, and bakes again when a light changes. Metal follows with T4b. The engine fills the list each frame from the 3D nodes that are lights. A 3D scene's ambient multiplies its sky light. This was researched against several engines: Unity URP: Light2D, and forward's light list per object. Godot 4: CanvasModulate, PointLight2D, 8+8 lights per mesh on mobile. Bevy. The PICA200's fragment lighting. Alternatives not taken : Drawing lights as translucent halos with no light picture (option A). It is cheap, but light cannot darken what it does not cover, nor multiply colours. A light per sprite computed on the processor. It does not scale, and the 3DS has a GPU for it. Tasks [x] T1 — draw2d : the light layer's commands and their tests · go-renderer · R1, R2 [x] T2 — OpenGL: the light target and its blend; pixels compared · go-renderer · R1, R3 [x] T3 — GL ES: the same for Android and the web · go-renderer · R3 [x] T4 — 3DS: the light target in citro3d; Azahar captures, and a measure · go-renderer · R3, R6 [x] T4b — Metal: the light target and its blends, unbuilt here · go-renderer · R3 [x] T5 — scenefile and engine : lights on nodes, the ambient, drawn each frame without allocating · go-engine · R4, R6 [x] T6 — Level: the inspector (2D and 3D), the ambient, the radii and a mark for each light, Play lit · go-engine · R5 [x] T7 — Io World's start screen lit from Unity's lights · go-engine-io-world · R7 [x] T8 — A lighting lights only its clip, on every backend; the 3DS paints its ambient instead of clearing it · go-renderer · R10 [x] T9 — 3D point lights: scene , the choice in sceneplan , OpenGL and GL ES shading · go-renderer · R8, R9 [x] T10 — 3D lights baked on the 3DS · go-renderer · R8 [x] T11 — The engine's 3D lights and ambient; the audit's 2D fixes (culling, node scale, one screen rectangle) · go-engine · R8, R9 Result Built on go-renderer's dev (feature/lights merged with feature/3ds-moving-light), go-engine's feature/lights and Io World's main . Each requirement's check, as run: Id Check Result R1 draw2d and painter tests; OpenGL pixel tests pass R2 a test per kind; pixels for point and sprite lights pass R3 OpenGL and WebGL (Chromium) pixels; Azahar captures; Metal pass, but Metal: written, unbuilt (the author on a Mac) R4 engine tests: light on nodes, ambient, scale, hidden, out of sight pass R5 editor tests; captures of Level in 2D and 3D pass R6 allocation tests (2D frame, sync, choosing); eight lights at 60 FPS in Azahar pass; the console is still to be measured R7 Io World's test; captures in the editor and in Azahar pass; the author on the console R8 sceneplan and engine tests; OpenGL pixels; captures on WebGL and the 3DS pass R9 the choice's tests, with instances; the allocation test pass R10 a pixel test on OpenGL; a capture of both 3DS screens pass What the author still has to review or check: Metal was written on Linux and never built: go test ./metal on a Mac compiles its shaders. The console: frame times with eight 2D lights, and a lamp moving over baked meshes. On the 3DS , a node marked Moving is not lit by lamps. A floor shows a lamp's pool only where it has vertices. GL ES lights the screen only, like its backdrops (no offscreen capture). Changes beyond the proposal: a body's copy no longer shares its zone's pull (with a test); the unknown body kind's message; the broken GLB test deleted at the author's word; a one-frame flicker of backdrops fixed in OpenGL. It was researched against Unity URP's Light2D, Godot 4 (CanvasModulate, PointLight2D, mobile's light limits), Bevy and the PICA200's fragment lighting. A sister session audited it, and its findings are in: clip, culling, node scale, banding, the order of lights. It was reviewed after, and the review's findings were fixed, except the GL ES framebuffer (noted above).

proposals/editor-trust.title: 3. Undo, several nodes, sharp pixels: an editor to trust
proposals/editor-trust.text: 3. Undo, several nodes, sharp pixels: an editor to trust Status: done · Author's approval: proposal ☑ plan ☑ (2026-10-18, "haz todas pero además haz que aparezca la versión en la ventana de editor y logs": approved together) Why Proposal 2 left four things out on purpose: undo, choosing several nodes, pixel art drawn sharp, and a 3D Level like the 2D one. Without undo, one wrong click loses work. One node at a time makes ten coins ten jobs. Pixel art drawn blurred misleads about how the game looks. And nobody can tell which Go Engine an editor or a game was built with. What Id Requirement Check R1 The editor's window, its top bar and the logs of the editor, the game and the go-engine command say which Go Engine they run: its release and commit, and whether it is a local copy test the version says which Go Engine it is ; test a local Go Engine gives its commit to the build R2 Every change to the scene can be undone and redone (Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Shift+Z, and buttons); a drag or a stretch of typing is one step tests a change is undone and redone , a drag is one step to undo R3 Several nodes can be chosen (Shift in the tree and the view); dragging moves them together, Delete and Duplicate act on all tests shift adds a node to the choice and takes it out , deleting and duplicating act on every node chosen , dragging moves every node chosen R4 The mouse in the 2D view does what the tools say: drags, right-button erasing, the hand, fill tests that press, move and let go the buttons over the view R5 Pixel art is drawn sharp: pictures of a 2D scene are scaled to the nearest pixel, on the desktop and the 3DS a test of go-renderer's sampling; captures R6 Level's tool rail is the same in 3D: Select and Hand, the others greyed capture Out of scope Undoing changes to sprite and tileset files (Art saves them itself). Choosing several nodes by dragging a box. Design Version (done first): engine.Version() reads the program's build information. For a local copy (a go.work or a folder replace ), go-engine passes the commit with -ldflags -X . Undo : the editor keeps the scene's description after each change, in a list with a place in it. Undo builds the scene again from the one before, keeping the chosen nodes by path. Changes within half a second of each other are one step, so a drag or typing a number is undone at once. Several nodes : Editor.Chosen holds the nodes besides Selected , the one the inspector shows. Sharp pixels : go-renderer's 2D pictures get a filter setting. A 2D scene draws its sprites and tiles with the nearest pixel. That change belongs to go-renderer, on its feature/3ds branch, committed only with the author's say. Tasks [x] T1 — the version, in the editor's window, its top bar and the logs · engine/ , project/ , editor/ , cmd/ · R1 · tests: the version says which Go Engine it is , a local Go Engine gives its commit to the build [x] T2 — undo and redo · editor/ · R2 · tests: a change is undone and redone , a drag is one step to undo [x] T3 — several nodes chosen · editor/ · R3 · tests: shift adds a node to the choice and takes it out , deleting and duplicating act on every node chosen , dragging moves every node chosen [x] T4 — the 2D view's mouse, tested · editor/ · R4 [x] T5 — Level's tool rail in 3D · editor/ · R6 [x] T6 — sharp pixel art · go-renderer draw2d , opengl , ctr ; engine/ · R5 Result Built. The version of Go Engine shows in the editor's title and top bar. The logs of the editor, the game and the go-engine command say it too, with the commit of a local copy and whether it has changes. Undo and redo of every change to the scene. A drag or a number typed is one step. Several nodes chosen with Shift, then dragged, deleted and duplicated together. Tests that press, move and let go the mouse over the 2D view. Level's tool rail in 3D (Select and Hand). Pixel art drawn sharp, through go-renderer's draw2d.Image.Sharp (feature/3ds 3b08cd9, committed with the author's say). The engine sets it on every sprite, frame and tile. Checked. Every task's tests pass. Sharp pixels were compared before and after in captures, on the desktop and in the 3DS emulator. Not done. Metal draws sharp pictures blended, as before: it is hand-written and was not touched. Changes to sprite and tileset files are not undone (Art saves them itself). Choosing nodes with a box was out of scope. For a person. Undo after real edits, Shift-clicks and drags with a real mouse.

proposals/editor-workspaces.title: 2. Editor workspaces: one task at a time
proposals/editor-workspaces.text: 2. Editor workspaces: one task at a time Status: done · Author's approval: proposal ☑ plan ☑ (2026-10-18, "sigue hasta tener todo implementado": approved together, while away) Why The editor is one screen that does six jobs at once. With a coin chosen, the inspector asks for its place in the level, the cut and timing of its picture, and its code. The top bar offers testing, building and the project. A level designer scrolls past animation settings on every coin. An artist has no screen of their own. A solo developer is offered every job at every moment. DaVinci Resolve answers this with pages, one screen per stage of the work. The study behind this change is "Editor workspaces", a private page of the author's. What Id Requirement Check R1 A bar along the bottom switches between six workspaces (Project, Art, Level, Code, Play, Build), each with an icon and a word, and the keys 1–6 when no field is being typed in; the open scene and the chosen node stay the same across them test switching workspaces keeps the scene and the choice ; capture of each workspace R2 Pictures become sprites and tilesets of their own: a .sprite.json (picture, frames, animations) and a .tileset.json (picture, tile size, solid tiles) that nodes and tile maps point to, so ten coins share one spin; scenes written before still open tests a node plays the animations of the sprite it points to , a tile map takes its solid tiles from its tileset , a sheet of its own wins over its sprite's file R3 Art: the project's sprites and tilesets in a list, the picture large with its cut drawn over it, frames chosen by clicking, animations in a strip with a preview, tiles made solid by clicking; a picture becomes a sprite or a tileset with one action tests a picture becomes a sprite with its frames , clicked frames make an animation , a clicked tile turns solid and back , an edited sprite is saved and read back R4 Level: a tool rail beside the view (Select, Paint, Erase, Fill, Hand) with keys V, B, E, G, H; bodies, tile cells and camera bounds drawn on demand; the palette shows the tileset as drawn; the inspector only places (2D transform, sprite and first animation, body, behaviour values) tests the paint tool paints and the select tool chooses , fill paints the region of the tile clicked , the palette keeps the tileset's columns ; captures R5 Play: the game at the shape of a target (16:9 or the 3DS's top screen), with pause, a step of one frame and a restart; the chosen node watched live (position, velocity, on the floor, animation, behaviour fields); the game's log under it tests a paused game stands still and steps one frame , restart starts the scene as written , the watch shows a behaviour's fields ; captures R6 Project: the assets as a grid of thumbnails with folders and filters, a preview that says where each is used, scenes as items that open in Level, and the project's settings tests an asset's uses are found in every scene , settings are saved ; capture R8 Build: one card per target (this computer, the 3DS) with its last result, size and time, its actions and its own log test a build's result is kept per target ; capture R9 Icons say what they do: one meaning per icon, a word beside any icon not known by everyone test no icon stands for two things R10 The demo uses the new assets: its coins share one sprite and its levels one tileset the demo's tests pass; capture of its coin in Art Out of scope A code editor inside the editor (Zed is the project's code editor). Undo and redo, choosing several nodes, sharp pixel art (a go-renderer filter). The first study found them; they belong to their own changes. 3D scenes in Art (models are not cut or animated here). 3D keeps today's Level view. Documentation chapters: v0.0.1 is not documented yet. Design Workspaces in the editor. Editor.Workspace is a small type with the six values, set with SetWorkspace . Entering Play plays the scene, and leaving it stops. View.Build draws three things: the top bar (project, scene, saved state), the chosen workspace's panels, and the workspace bar with the status line. Each workspace is its own file of panels ( workspace_project.go , workspace_art.go , …). What is shared (tree, inspector sections) stays where it is. Code says "workspace" because "mode" already means 2D or 3D. Sprites and tilesets as assets ( scenefile ). They are read and checked like scenes: Sprite{Picture, Columns, Rows, Animations, Start} in *.sprite.json . Tileset{Picture, TileSize, Solid} in *.tileset.json . A node's sprite may name a picture (as today) or a sprite file. A tile map's tileset may name a picture (with its own tile size and solid tiles, as today) or a tileset file. The engine resolves them once, when a scene is built, through its asset cache. An inline sheet still works and wins, so old scenes play. Alternatives not taken: Moving every sheet into files at once: it breaks scenes. Resources per scene: the coins of two levels would still disagree. Art edits these files through editor/art.go . It has no interface in it, so it is tested. It makes a sprite or tileset from a picture, sets the cut, and adds, renames and removes animations. It adds a clicked frame, toggles a solid tile, and saves. Its panels: the list; the canvas: the picture with its cut, frames numbered; the cut and collision, on the right; the animation strip with a preview, underneath. Level gets a Tool (select, paint, erase, fill, hand) instead of the paint checkbox. It also gets an overlay switch for bodies and camera bounds, and the tile map's cell grid while it is chosen. A flood fill and a palette in the tileset's own columns join them. The inspector loses what moved elsewhere: the sheet and animations, now in Art (it shows the sprite, a "Starts with" choice and a button to open it in Art); the tile size and solid tiles, now in the tileset; Go types in behaviour fields; the 3D/2D tab, moved to Project's scene settings. Play uses the editor's play-in-the-view, with Pause , StepFrame and Restart . It adds a target shape and a watch of the chosen node, whose exported behaviour fields are read by reflection. A log is fed by an slog handler the editor installs while playing. Project , Code and Build are lists and details over what the editor already knows: Project.AssetTree , Project.Behaviours , the scenes' descriptions (to find uses), and the builds it runs (kept per target). Icons are named constants in editor/icons.go , one per meaning. A test checks that no two meanings share an icon. Sprites and tilesets are files of their own. The engine reads them once, and nodes and tile maps point to them. A node may name the animation it starts with, so nodes that share a sprite start differently. The editor is six workspaces along a bottom bar (keys 1 to 6, in Play too): Level: a tool rail, fill, overlays, a palette in the tileset's columns, and an inspector that only places (with "Starts with"). Art: the picture large with its cut numbered, frames clicked into animations, a preview, and solid tiles. Play: pause, a step, a restart, a screen's shape, a live watch of the scene playing, and the log. Project: thumbnails, filters, uses and settings. Each workspace was captured with the demo open, on the author's private progress page (docs are not written for v0.0.1). The demo was played in Azahar. Review. The reviewer's findings were fixed: The play log gives the log package back, and is only taken when a game starts. Opening a scene or an Art file over unsaved changes is refused. A shared sprite is never written over, and builds save first. Only Level and Play take the view's input. Play's tree is the scene playing. Open in Art opens that node's sprite. A sprite file chosen drops the node's own sheet. The screen's shape is offered for 2D games only. Rebuilding's errors show in Code. Code reads the scenes at most every two seconds. Sprites, tilesets and clearing have icons of their own. New error codes have tests. Not done. Undo and redo, choosing several nodes, and sharp pixel art (a go-renderer filter), as the proposal said. In a 3D scene, Level keeps its old view. For a person. Use the mouse: painting and filling, dragging in Select, clicking frames and tiles in Art, the palette. The tests cover the model and one simulated click. Nobody has painted a level by hand yet.

proposals/games-driven-by-code.text: 9. 3D games driven by code Status: done, pending the author's review · Author's approval: proposal ☑ (2026-10-21, "Okay") plan ☑ (2026-10-21, "Si") Why The engine serves games whose scenes are arranged in the editor: models from .glb files, cameras placed by hand, keys for input. An online 3D game made mostly in code needs more. Its vehicles are built from designs at run time. They move every frame. Its effects glow or fade. Its camera chases the player. On the 3DS it uses the slider's depth, both screens, and every control the console has. On the desktop it captures the mouse. It ships for Windows and macOS. Without these, such a game has to skip the engine and draw with Go Renderer on its own. One game is waiting on them now; every 3D game in code will want them. What In the order that unblocks the most. Each requirement can come out in its own version. Id Requirement Check R1 A behaviour gives a node a mesh it built at run time, and gives it another later; the old one is let go of test a mesh set from code is drawn, and replacing it frees the old one R2 A node is marked as moving every frame, so it is lit on the GPU and not baked again on each turn on the 3DS test of the flag reaching Go Renderer; on the 3DS, a turning node at full frame rate R3 A mesh from code gets a material that is unlit, additive or translucent, and double-sided; its opacity changes from frame to frame test per kind; capture of each on the desktop and in Azahar R4 The game draws a 2D layer each frame over the 3D view: over the window on the desktop, over the top screen on the 3DS, in both eyes when stereo is on capture on the desktop; capture of both eyes in Azahar R5 A camera has its own far plane (up to thousands of metres) and field of view, set in the editor or from code test a camera's far plane is the one set R6 On the 3DS, the top screen is drawn in stereo, its depth following the slider; slider down is flat Azahar's stereo capture; by hand on a console R7 On the 3DS, the bottom screen shows a second 3D scene with its own camera, with a go-ui interface over it capture in Azahar R8 engine.Input gives the 3DS's circle pad, C-stick, gyroscope, ZL/ZR, L/R, START and touches on the bottom screen; on the desktop, the mouse's movement with the pointer captured, and the keys; each pressed this frame as well as held tests of each mapping with a made-up input state R9 A game runs code once a frame before the behaviours (a network exchange), and asks for something to run between frames (the 3DS's system keyboard, which takes both screens) test the frame's hook runs before every behaviour ; test of the call between frames R10 The 3DS loop yields once a frame, so Go Sound's buffers are filled on time a sound plays without crackles in Azahar with a slow frame R11 A game's releases carry desktop programs for Windows, macOS and Linux, as well as the one Build makes for this computer the workflow Build writes runs on GitHub and its programs start on each system Out of scope Networking itself: the game brings its own (Go for 3DS has TCP and TLS). Sound in the engine: the game uses Go Sound directly. R10 only keeps the loop fair to it. Editing meshes from code in the editor: they exist only while the game plays. Signing and notarising macOS programs, and Windows installers. A text field of the engine's own: a game shows go-ui's over the 3D window (R4's layer, for go-ui). Design What is there already Go UI's window on the 3DS already draws the top screen in stereo with the slider (R6), paints the scene's own drawing ( World.Overlay.Drawing ) in each eye (R4 on the 3DS), and yields each frame ( runtime.Gosched , R10). Go Renderer's nodes have Moving (R2), and its materials are lit, unlit, translucent and double-sided (most of R3). The engine only has to reach them. In the engine Meshes from code (R1, R2): Node.SetMesh(*scene.Mesh) replaces the node's geometry, and Node.SetMoving(bool) sets Go Renderer's flag on it, kept when a scene is copied for playing. Games use Go Renderer's scene.Mesh and scene.Material as they are: a type of the engine's own would only copy them. Camera (R5): scenefile.Camera gains near and far (metres; 0 keeps today's 0.05 and 2000), shown in the inspector. Node.Camera() and Node.SetCamera() let code change them. Over the 3D (R4): engine.SetOverlay(func(list *draw2d.List, width, height float32)) draws each frame over a 3D scene. It goes to Go UI's new SceneView.Drawing , which Go UI paints over the scene and under the interface on the desktop and phones (its window used to overwrite World.Overlay.Drawing with the interface), and on the 3DS's top screen in each eye. SetBottomScreen becomes SetInterface : the bottom screen on the 3DS, over the window elsewhere (login fields). Below, in 3D (R7): engine.SetSecondScreen(scene) gives the 3DS's bottom screen a scene of its own, with the interface over it. Input (R8): engine.Input gains Stick() , CStick() , Gyroscope() , Touches() and MouseMovement() ; L, R, ZL, ZR and START become keys with Down and Pressed . SetPointerCaptured(bool) hides and holds the desktop's pointer. Hooks (R9): engine.BeforeBehaviours(func(context *Context)) runs first in each step, with the frame's context (its Node nil), in the game and in the editor's Play. engine.BetweenFrames(func()) runs once at the start of the next step. On the 3DS that is outside the frame being drawn, where the system keyboard can take both screens. Releases (R11): Build gains "Release workflow". It writes .github/workflows/release.yml into the game: Go builds the game on GitHub's Windows, macOS and Linux machines and attaches each program to a release. Building for another system from Linux is not taken: GLFW needs cgo, and so a C compiler and the system's own libraries for each target. In the author's libraries (each on a feature/ branch, with the author's permission) Go Renderer : Material.Additive (light adds to what is behind: beams, sparks) in OpenGL, Metal and ctr. The C-stick and the gyroscope in ctr.Reading , as Go for 3DS reads them. Go UI : SceneView.Below (a scene and camera for the bottom screen, the interface painted over it), Options.KeepStart (START reaches the game instead of quitting), and a scene's LockCursor passed on to the window (Go Renderer's window loop applies it). Versions Each version leaves the engine working and can be used by a game at once. on Android the game's interface is not shown yet (the touch buttons fill the window) [x] T8 — Go UI ( feature/scene-drawing ): SceneView.Below , Options.KeepStart , and a scene's LockCursor reaching the window (Go Renderer's input already captures the pointer, so no option was needed) · R7, R8 · Go UI's tests; built for the 3DS through the engine's example [x] T9 — Go Renderer ( feature/motion-controls ): StartMotionControls , Reading.CStick() and Reading.Gyroscope · R8 · test of the C-stick's dead zone; built with TinyGo; on a console by hand [x] T10 — SetSecondScreen : it plays, and is seen from its main camera · engine/secondscreen.go · R7 · test the bottom scene plays and is seen from its camera ; a look in Azahar is pending [x] T11 — Input.Stick , RightStick , Gyroscope , SecondScreenTouch , MouseMovement ; shoulders, triggers and START as ButtonLeftShoulder … keys; SetPointerCaptured ; keepStart in engine.json · engine/controls.go, engine/console.go · R8 · tests of each mapping [x] T12 — the release workflow from Build ("Release workflow" on This computer's card), refused for a game on a local go-engine · project/release.go, editor · R11 · tests the release workflow builds for each system , a release of a game on a local engine is refused ; the YAML parses; a run on GitHub is pending, in a game's repository Result After the build, at the author's word ("the 3DS's things should be generic"), the engine's names say what a control or a screen is on any device, not on the 3DS: SetSecondScreen , RightStick , SecondScreenTouch , engine.Turn , ButtonLeftShoulder and the rest. The editor's Play also shows a 3D game at its screen's shape, with the second screen under the 3DS's hinge (Go Renderer feature/scene-area : DrawIn ; Go UI feature/scene-area : scene areas). Built, on feature/ branches until the author merges and releases them: go-engine feature/engine : R1–R5 and R7–R9 in the engine, R11's workflow, and examples/lighthouse . Seen working in the editor's Play and in Azahar at 60 frames a second. Go Renderer feature/motion-controls (with feature/additive in it): Material.Additive and the C-stick and gyroscope. The review found 14 things: all fixed, among them the stick's sign ( Input.Move read the stick's forward the wrong way before this change too), the frame hook running again for the bottom screen's scene (hooks now run in Scene.PlayFrame , the main scene's frame), and the gyroscope left on when its coefficient could not be read. Still to be checked by a person: Metal's additive pipeline, written on Linux, on a Mac. The sound with a slow frame on a console (R10), and the stereo, C-stick and gyroscope there. A run of the release workflow on GitHub; its YAML was checked by hand (a test that parses it would need a YAML library, not taken without asking). An early commit of the sample carried its editor's binary ( examples/lighthouse/build ); a later one removed it, but it stays in the history unless the author wants it rewritten.
