Go for 3DS and Go Sound (R7, R8)

proposals/generic-names.text: 10. Names for any device Status: done, pending the author's review · Author's approval: proposal ☑ (2026-10-21, "Si") plan ☑ (2026-10-21, "Si") Why The guidelines now ask for generic functions: named, and shaped, for what they do on any device, not for the first one that needed them, as nobody knows how they will be used later. An audit of the author's Go libraries found nine places that break it. Most of them are in go-engine's building and running for each target, and in the word "console" standing for the 3DS. A second console, or a game pad's right stick, would already have nowhere to go. Nothing of go-engine's is used by others yet beyond its own sample and one game in development, so this is the cheapest moment to rename. What Id Requirement Check R1 Input.RightStick reads the second stick of whatever device has one: a New 3DS's C-stick, and a game pad's right stick on a computer tests with a made-up 3DS reading and a made-up game pad state R2 A project builds, sends, plays and stops a game for a target through one set of functions that take the target ( Build(target) , SendTo(target) , PlayOn(target) , StopOn(target) ), instead of one function per device tests per target with the tools faked; the editor's Build cards call only these R3 A game has one application id ( applicationId in engine.json), which each target turns into what it needs; androidId is still read, so older projects keep working test an old androidId is read as the application id R4 Accepting a tool's licence is one set of functions that take the tool ( ReadLicence , Licence , AcceptLicence , DeclineLicence ), not Android's own test of the licence flow through the generic functions R5 "Console" no longer stands for the 3DS: names that mean the 3DS say so ( Nintendo3DSTarget , the 3DS's emulator), and names that are general become general ( DeviceAddress , SendToDevice ); engine.json's consoleAddress is still read tests of the renamed settings; an old engine.json still opens R6 SetBottomScreen is removed, and Settings.SceneMenu 's comment describes a general scene menu go vet ; the reference shows no 3DS words in general names R7 Go Sound: a sound output that cannot start returns one general error, ErrOutputUnavailable , defined on every system; on the 3DS it is returned when the DSP cannot start test in Go Sound that a program checking it builds everywhere; built for the 3DS R8 Go for 3DS: the bottom package becomes secondscreen , matching the engine Go for 3DS's tests; the 3DS sample builds R9 The engine's code and docs are checked again with the audit's search, and nothing general is named after one device the audit run again finds nothing in the engine Out of scope Packages that exist for one platform only (Go Renderer's ctr , Go for 3DS's own) keep their platform's names inside. New targets: this only makes room for them. Error codes across Go Sound: it uses plain sentinel errors throughout, which is its own change. Keeping the old names as aliases. Nothing is released with them except go-engine v0.0.x, which is still experimental. The two settings in engine.json are read under both names, because they live in people's files. Design Go Renderer: a game pad on a computer (R1) input.State gains RightStickX and RightStickY , as StickX and StickY are for the main stick. The desktop's window loop reads the first game pad GLFW knows ( GetGamepadState , which maps every pad to one layout) into both sticks, each with a dead zone. The 3DS's ctr.Controls puts the C-stick into the right stick once the motion controls are on. Go Renderer's feature/ branch, as before. go-engine Sticks (R1): Input.RightStick reads RightStickX and RightStickY , whatever filled them; the engine's own reading of the C-stick goes. Targets (R2, R5): the project package gets a Target type ( Desktop , Nintendo3DS , Android ) with Build , PlayOn , PlayInEmulator and StopOn , each choosing the target's way inside: today's Build3DS , SendTo3DS , BuildAndroid , PlayOnAndroid , StopOnAndroid , EmulatorCommand and PlayCommand become their private parts. Sending to the 3DS is playing there, as its Homebrew Launcher starts what it is sent (built: the plan's separate SendTo was one verb too many). A target without something (an emulator of its own) is refused with a code. The editor's BuildTarget becomes project.Target , and ConsoleTarget becomes Nintendo3DS ; the editor's PlayOn(target) and PlayInEmulator(target) replace PlayInWindow , PlayOnDevice , SendToConsole and the old PlayInEmulator . Settings (R3, R5): Settings.ApplicationID ( applicationId ) and Settings.DeviceAddress ( deviceAddress ). Reading engine.json takes androidId and consoleAddress when the new names are missing, and saving writes only the new ones. Tools (R5): build.Tools.ConsoleEmulator becomes Nintendo3DSEmulator ( nintendo3dsEmulator in tools.json, the old name still read); and the Play workspace's ConsoleScreen shape becomes Nintendo3DSScreens . Licences (R4): the editor's licence sheet takes a tool's name; Android's SDK is today's only tool with one. Leftovers (R6): SetBottomScreen goes; SceneMenu 's comment is made general. Go for 3DS and Go Sound (R7, R8) Each on a feature/ branch: Go for 3DS's bottom package is renamed secondscreen , its sample with it; Go Sound defines ErrOutputUnavailable in sound.go , and the 3DS's output returns it. Alternatives not taken Aliases for the old function names: they would keep the old names alive in new code. One Do(target, action) : four verbs read better, and each has its own errors. Tasks [x] T1 — Go Renderer: RightStickX / RightStickY , the desktop's game pad into both sticks, the C-stick into the right one · R1 · tests of the dead zone and the mapping with a made-up pad state [x] T2 — Input.RightStick from the right stick · engine/controls.go · R1 · test with a made-up state [x] T3 — project.Target with Build , PlayOn , PlayInEmulator , StopOn ; the old functions made private · project · R2 · tests per target; a target that cannot be sent to says so by its code [x] T4 — the editor on project.Target : PlayOn(target) , PlayInEmulator(target) , Nintendo3DSScreens · editor · R2, R5 · the editor's tests [x] T5 — applicationId , deviceAddress , nintendo3dsEmulator , the old names still read · engine/run.go, internal/build/tools.go · R3, R5 · tests an old androidId is read as the application id , and the same for the others [x] T6 — generic licences · editor/install.go · R4 · test of the licence flow [x] T7 — SetBottomScreen removed, SceneMenu 's comment · engine · R6 · go vet [x] T8 — Go Sound ErrOutputUnavailable · R7 · test; built for the 3DS [x] T9 — Go for 3DS bottom → secondscreen · R8 · its tests; its sample built [x] T10 — the audit again, and the reference and docs regenerated · R9 · the audit's search finds nothing in the engine Result Built, on feature/ branches until the author merges them: go-engine feature/engine : R1–R6 and R9. The second screen's guide is now docs/5-guides/8-the-second-screen.md . Go Renderer feature/game-pad (on feature/scene-area ): a computer's game pad into both sticks, and the 3DS's C-stick into the right one (R1). Go Sound feature/output-unavailable : ErrOutputUnavailable (R7). Go for 3DS feature/second-screen : the secondscreen package (R8). The review found 14 things, all fixed or answered here: the guide and test names that still said "bottom screen" or "console"; a stale comment; a test for a game sent with nothing to watch; the game pad made private, and letting its sticks go only when it is unplugged; targets outside the list given a name instead of a panic; Go Sound's failure made through one tested function. Two things stay as they are, for a person to judge: GLFW's game pad reading allocates while a pad is plugged in, because its Go binding returns a new state each time; avoiding it would need cgo of the engine's own. go-engine pins Go Renderer's unmerged feature/game-pad by pseudo-version: merge Go Renderer, Go UI, Go Sound and Go for 3DS first, then pin go-engine to their versions before it is released.

proposals/install-panel.title: 6. Install the tools from the editor
proposals/install-panel.text: 6. Install the tools from the editor Status: in progress · Author's approval: proposal ☑ plan ☑ (2026-10-18: "Todas"; tinygo-3ds commit, push and release allowed) Why Proposal 5 lets a person say where TinyGo, devkitPro, a 3DS emulator and Android's SDK and NDK are; they still have to find, download and install each by hand, and TinyGo for the 3DS is a fork with no binaries for anyone but its author. A person who has the editor should get a game onto their console or phone without leaving it. What Id Requirement Check R1 tinygo-3ds publishes releases with a TinyGo that needs nothing installed (LLVM inside), for Linux, and macOS and Windows when their builds pass the release's files; one run on a machine with no LLVM R2 tinygo-3ds finds devkitPro in $DEVKITPRO (as devkitPro's own tools do), /opt/devkitpro when unset test in tinygo-3ds; a 3DS build with devkitPro elsewhere R3 Install beside TinyGo downloads the release for this system into the user's data folder, checks it against its checksum, and sets TinyGo's place tests with a fake server: a release is downloaded, checked and set , a release that does not match its checksum is refused R4 Install beside devkitPro runs devkitPro's own installer for the 3DS ( dkp-pacman -S 3ds-dev ) in a terminal, as it asks for the system's password; without dkp-pacman, it opens devkitPro's install guide test of the command asked for; by hand on Linux R5 Install beside the Android SDK downloads Google's command-line tools and, once the person has read and accepted Android's licences in the panel, installs platform-tools, build-tools, a platform and the NDK tests with a fake server and a fake sdkmanager R6 Install beside the 3DS emulator downloads Azahar's release for this system (the AppImage on Linux, the zip of its program on a Mac and Windows), checked by the SHA-256 GitHub gives test with a fake server R7 The panel shows each install's progress and what it said; installs run one at a time, and the builds wait capture Out of scope Installing Go or a JDK (the editor runs with Go; Android's tools need Java: the panel says so). Updating what is installed (Install again does it). devkitPro's packages downloaded one by one: their servers and packages (zstd) are devkitPro's installer's to handle. Design tinygo-3ds : a workflow on main that runs TinyGo's own release build ( make release STATIC=1 ) on Linux, macOS and Windows and attaches the archives and their SHA-256 to a release ( v0.42.0-3ds.N ). The target's devkitPro paths become {devkitpro} , which the builder fills from $DEVKITPRO . go-engine internal/install : a download (HTTP, with progress), a checksum, and unpacking of .tar.gz and .zip (standard library only), into go-engine/ of os.UserCacheDir 's sibling data folder. One function per tool returns the place to set. The editor runs installs as it runs builds ( Editor.Run ), shows progress under the tool, and saves the place found. proposals/io-world-on-the-3ds.title: 7. Pushing, riding and pulling: io-world on the 3DS
proposals/io-world-on-the-3ds.text: 7. Pushing, riding and pulling: io-world on the 3DS Status: done (the console check is the author's) · Author's approval: proposal ☑ plan ☑ (2026-10-19, "sigue": together; the io-world repository private) Why io-world is a small puzzle-platformer made with Godot 3. It has one level of 100-pixel tiles and a player of three pictures (body, tail, eyes). It has jump pads, a magnet the player pushes and stands on, a platform on a rail, and a magnetic field that pulls the other way. Made again from nothing in Go Engine and played on the 3DS, it answers two questions. Can a person make a game from scratch with the editor? And what does the engine still lack? The engine's physics has three kinds of body: solids that never move, moving bodies that only meet solids, and triggers. Three of io-world's mechanics need more, and any puzzle-platformer will want the same: Something to push : a box the player pushes along the floor and stands on. Something to ride : a platform that moves and carries what stands on it. Somewhere gravity turns : an area where bodies fall another way. What Id Requirement Check R1 A pushable body falls like a moving one, stops against solids, holds up a moving body that stands on it, and is pushed by one that walks into it, until a solid stops both tests a body pushes a box until a wall stops both , a body stands on a box R2 A platform body moves at its velocity, ignores gravity and solids, carries the bodies standing on it, and pushes those in its way tests a platform carries what stands on it , a platform pushes a body in its way R3 A trigger with a gravity pulls the moving and pushable bodies inside it that way instead of the world's; "on the floor" is then the side it pulls them to tests a body falls the way its zone pulls , a body stands on the floor its gravity pulls it to R4 A behaviour changes the camera the scene is seen through by marking another one Main test marking another camera Main changes the view R5 The three kinds and the gravity are chosen in Level's inspector, and drawn over the view when bodies are shown capture R6 io-world, made with the editor (Art, Level, Code), plays on the 3DS: walk, jump, jump pads, the magnet, the rail and the field the author on the console; captures from Azahar R7 What was hard while making it is written down, to become the next proposals the list in this proposal's Result Out of scope Bodies that turn, slopes, and shapes other than boxes. io-world's sounds, menus and levels beyond its first. Converting Godot scenes in the editor: a one-off script, kept in the game's own repository, as the platformer demo's was. Design Physics ( physics ): two new kinds beside Solid , Moving and Trigger . Pushable moves as Moving does. A moving body that runs into it along X moves it, by as much as it is not blocked; a chain of boxes moves together. Along Y it stops the body, which stands on it. Solids stop it as they stop any moving body. Platform moves by its velocity before the others each step. Bodies whose feet rest on it move with it, and a body in its way is moved out of it, as a pushable is. A trigger's Gravity , when set, replaces the world's for the bodies inside it during that step. A body knows which way gravity pulled it, and OnFloor means "stopped going that way". The order of a step: platforms, then moving and pushable bodies, then triggers. Scene files : BodyKind gains "pushable" and "platform" . Body gains gravity: [x, y] , read for triggers. Editor : Level's body inspector offers the five kinds, and a gravity field for triggers. The body overlay draws a platform's direction and a zone's arrow. io-world : a new repository, made with go-engine new . The art comes from io-world's PNGs through Art: sprites, and a tileset of 100-pixel tiles. The level is drawn in Level, or converted once from Level1.tscn by a script in the repository. Its behaviours in Go: Player : run, jump, reset. Jumper : a push along its direction. Rail : a platform going back and forth. Field : a gravity zone the player can turn. The cameras. It is built with tinygo-3ds from Build's Install, and sent with 3dslink. Branches : the engine's part on feature/physics , from feature/engine , where the other session's work is. io-world goes in its own repository. Tasks [x] T1 — pushable bodies · physics , scenefile , engine · R1 · tests of R1 [x] T2 — platforms · physics , scenefile , engine · R2 · tests of R2 [x] T3 — gravity zones · physics , scenefile , engine · R3 · tests of R3 [x] T4 — switching cameras, tested · engine · R4 [x] T5 — the kinds and the gravity in Level · editor · R5 · capture [x] T6 — io-world: project, art, level, behaviours · new repository · R6 · captures [x] T7 — io-world on the 3DS, and the list of what was hard · R6, R7 [x] T8 — asked while building: a menu of the scenes on the 3DS's bottom screen ( sceneMenu ), and SetBottomScreen for a game to draw it its own way · engine , editor · tests the menu lists the scenes by their names , a game's own bottom screen is given its scenes Result Built. Two new kinds of body, pushable and platform , and gravity zones (a trigger's pull ). They are in the physics, the scene files and Level's inspector, each drawn its own way. A body's floor is the side its gravity pulls it to. Pushing goes across that gravity, in a row of at most eight, and never round a ring. A platform carries the stacks standing on it, pushes what is in its way, and stops against what it cannot move. Triggers notice pushable bodies too. On the 3DS, a menu of the scenes on the bottom screen ( sceneMenu ), or the game's own ( SetBottomScreen ). Io World has io-world's first level, and its dev branch's version: a button that starts a rail that waits, and a cube. A menu of levels is made of the game's own pieces. It was sent to the author's 3DS by FTP. It now lives in io-world 's own repository, in its IoWorldGo/ folder. Checked. Every requirement's tests pass: the physics', the engine's allocations with the new kinds, and the editor's. Io World's own tests cover landing, running, pads, the magnet, the rail, the field, the button and the cube. The editor was captured, and the game in Azahar, with the menu changing the level by a touch. Not done. Bodies that turn, slopes, tiles' own shapes and flipped tiles. io-world's attractor tiles are partial polygons, here whole squares; flipped tiles are drawn unflipped. The original's two fixed screens became one camera that follows Io. At 400 pixels, a whole screen's width made the tiles 14 pixels. What was hard, making it (for the next proposals): The editor was not where it was made. The level came from a script ( tools/convert_level.py ), and the behaviours from a code editor. The editor opened, played and changed it. Drawing a 90-by-37 level of 100-pixel tiles by hand, and five jump pads, would take an afternoon: there are no prefabs to place again and again. Prefabs. io-world's jump pad, rail and button are small scenes placed many times. Here each is written out in full. Instancing a scene in another is the biggest missing piece. Sprites made of tiles. The pad and the rail are rows of a tile picture. Art cannot compose them, so the script did, into new pictures. One tileset per tile map. Godot's tile set mixes pictures: one level became two tile maps. Touching needs overlapping. A pad's trigger, level with the ground it is on, never notices what stands on it: it has to reach above it. Easy to get wrong, and silent. go-engine new opens the editor , so it needs a display. Making a project on a server needed project.Create from Go. (Fixed later: go-engine new -open=false only makes it.) Choices the original left open. The field pulled left in the level and up in its prefab, and worked in neither. The button only printed. Here the field pulls up (the inspector changes it), and the button starts the rail, as io-world's first, Unity version did. The original's other scenes. io-world began in Unity, with Demoivania and MainMenu . Demoivania (December 2022) had a menu with music and lights, and a long level with levels 2 and 3 started. It had buttons, a cube, rails, magnets, liquids and another character, with about 710 brick sprites and 30 C# scripts. They went away when it moved to Godot, which only ever had Level1 . They could come here too, as a later proposal. For a person. Play both levels on the console: the controls, the rail and the field's feel, and the menu under a thumb.

proposals/phones-and-consoles.title: 4. Phones and consoles: build, send and play from the editor
proposals/phones-and-consoles.text: 4. Phones and consoles: build, send and play from the editor Status: done · Author's approval: proposal ☑ plan ☑ (2026-10-18, "funciona en ds haz lo de ds y añade un export para android y un modo para jugar por adb": approved together) Why The demo plays on the 3DS, but getting it there is work outside the editor: build, copy the .3dsx, start the Homebrew Launcher. Android is not offered at all, though go-ui runs there (go-ui-android). A game is tried where it will be played, so the editor should take it there. What Id Requirement Check R1 A 2D game draws on Android, and a phone held upright sees the whole width the camera asks for test a narrow screen sees more height to keep the camera's width ; capture R2 On a touch screen the game shows buttons (left, right, A, B) that hold the keys the console's do test a finger on a touch button holds its key R3 The Build workspace builds an Android package (.apk) of the game, without the editor, under an application id the project's settings keep tests an application id is made from the game's name , an Android build asks for the package R4 The Android card plays the game on the device adb sees: installs it, starts it, shows its log and stops it test playing on a device installs, starts and reads the log ; the emulator R5 The 3DS card sends the .3dsx to a console's Homebrew Launcher (3dslink) and opens it in an emulator when one is installed test sending to the console runs 3dslink with the program R6 Play's 3DS shape shows both screens: the game on the top one, the bottom one under it capture Out of scope Signing for a store (go-ui-apk's -release ): a debug package is for trying. Touch controls a game designs itself; the buttons are the console's, as keys. Choosing among several devices: the first one adb lists. Design Android build : go-ui-apk, run as a tool of the game's module ( go tool go-ui-apk ), at a version go-engine names. The build adds the tool, and the go-ui version go-engine uses, to the game's go.mod when missing. -tags release leaves the editor out. The package carries arm64 (phones) and x86_64 (the emulator on a PC). Playing on a device , through adb: adb install -r installs it. adb shell monkey starts the launcher activity. adb logcat -s Go streams into the card's log. adb shell am force-stop stops it. Touch buttons : on Android, the interface that paints the scene paints four buttons over its bottom corners. Each frame, the fingers over them set the keys, kept from frame to frame as on the console. Where the buttons go is one function of the screen's size, used to draw and to read. 3DS : 3dslink (devkitPro's tools) sends to the netloader (Y in the Homebrew Launcher). The emulator is Azahar, or Citra, found on the path. go-renderer : the GL ES shaders of sharp pictures did not link on Android, because a uniform was declared with different precisions. The fix is go-renderer's, committed with the author's say. A 2D game draws on Android. A 2D camera's width is the least it sees across. So an upright phone sees more height instead of losing the sides. The demo's 15.5 m keeps the 3DS's view as it was, and the Level view's camera frame follows the same rule. On a phone held upright, the game sits at the top at its camera's shape, with touch buttons under it (left, right, B, A). Held sideways, it fills the screen with the buttons over its corners. Every key of a plugged-in keyboard still reaches the game. proposals/platformer-demo.title: 1. A platformer demo that drives the engine
proposals/platformer-demo.text: 1. A platformer demo that drives the engine Status: done · Author's approval: proposal ☑ plan ☑ Why Go Engine (v0.0.1) can place things in a scene and run code on them. But nothing yet makes a game feel like one: things don't fall, collide, animate or get followed by the camera. A small platformer needs all of that. Building one tells us what the engine is missing, and proves each piece works on the desktop and on the 3DS. The author's own godot-generic-platformer is the reference for how it should play. What The engine gains generic 2D pieces any game can use. The demo is a project made with the editor that uses them, with only its own behaviours as game code. Id Requirement Check R1 A body falls with gravity and stands on solid ground; it never passes through a solid, at any frame rate test a falling body lands on the ground and stays there ; test a fast body does not pass through a thin wall R2 A body slides along walls and floors instead of stopping dead, and knows whether it stands on the floor test a body pushed into a wall slides up it ; test a body on the ground is on the floor R3 A level is painted in the editor from a tileset picture onto a grid, and its solid tiles collide in the editor, paint tiles and play: the player stands on them; test solid tiles stop a body R4 A sprite plays named animations from a sprite sheet (idle, walk, jump), at a set speed, and faces left or right test an animation shows each frame for its time and loops ; the demo's player walks and turns R5 The camera follows a node smoothly and stays inside the level's bounds test the camera follows its target and stops at the level's edge R6 Triggers: something happens when the player touches a node (a coin is collected, spikes restart the level, a flag goes to the next level) test touching a trigger is reported once ; the demo's coins, spikes and flag R7 The demo plays the same on the desktop and the 3DS: arrows or the cross move, Space, the up arrow, A or up on the cross jumps play it in the editor, in a window, and on the 3DS emulator; the author plays it on the console R8 Everything the demo needs from the engine is generic: no part of the engine knows it is a platformer review: the engine's new code names no coin, spike or player Out of scope Slopes, one-way platforms, moving platforms and ladders (later, if the demo grows). Enemies with their own behaviour, shooting, bounce pads. Sound and music (Go Sound comes in a later change), menus, a game interface, saving. 3D physics. Documentation of the new pieces: v0.0.1 is not documented yet. Decisions Art : the sprites and tilesets of godot-generic-platformer , as the author allowed. The demo says where they come from. Where : examples/platformer/ , a project with its own go.mod , beside the engine. Each change to the engine is played with it in the same commit. Scope : one world, the forest, in three short levels. Lava and snow come later, from the same pieces. Design Four generic pieces join the engine. The demo only adds its behaviours, scenes and art. space ← physics ← engine ← editor 1. physics , a new package : boxes that move and collide in 2D, knowing nothing of nodes. A Body has a box (its size in metres), a velocity, a gravity scale and a kind. A solid never moves. A moving body falls and is pushed back by solids. A trigger only notices what touches it. World.Step(seconds) adds gravity, then moves each moving body one axis at a time. Its steps are no longer than half the body's smallest side, so a fast body cannot jump through a thin wall (R1). A body that hits a solid stops on that axis only and keeps the other: that is sliding (R2). Hitting a floor sets OnFloor . Overlaps of triggers are reported once, when they begin (R6). Alternatives not taken: a physics library (Box2D ports, Chipmunk). They bring rotation, joints and a dependency the demo doesn't need. Boxes lined up with the axes are what platformers use, and small enough to learn from. 2. Tiles, in engine and scenefile : a node may be a tile map (R3). It has a tileset picture, the size of a tile in pixels, a grid of tile numbers, and which tiles are solid. The tileset is cut into one picture per tile when it loads. So draw2d draws whole pictures, and Go Renderer needs no change. Solid tiles become solid bodies, rows of them merged into one box. A level of a thousand tiles is a few dozen boxes. The editor gains a tile tool in the 2D view. The tileset shows in the inspector to choose from; drag to paint, right-drag to erase. 3. Animated sprites, in engine and scenefile : a sprite may be a sheet of equal frames (R4). It has named animations (frames, frames per second, looping), and may face left. Frames are cut from the sheet when it loads. draw2d draws pictures upright, so facing left uses a mirrored copy made once. A behaviour calls node.Play("walk") and node.FaceLeft(true) . 4. Bodies, triggers, the camera and scenes, in engine : A node may have a body: "body": {"kind": "moving", "size": [0.8, 0.6]} in the scene file. The engine keeps the physics world in step with the nodes every frame. Behaviours update, the world steps, and nodes take their bodies' positions. A behaviour with Touched(context, other *Node) hears when its node's trigger begins touching another body (R6). A camera may follow a node, with a smoothing time, kept inside the level's bounds (R5). The bounds are the tile maps' extent, or bounds of its own. The tile maps bound the sides and the bottom. The sky above stays open, so the camera rises with a jump, unless the camera has a ceiling (a cave). context.RestartScene() and context.ChangeScene(file) let a game restart a level or go to the next (R6, R7). They work in a window, on the 3DS and in the editor's view. The demo , examples/platformer/ , is a project like any other: its go.mod points at the engine beside it. Its behaviours are these: Player : walk, jump with Space or A, animations, facing. Coin : collected when touched. Hazard : spikes and water restart the level. Flag : goes to the next level. It has three forest levels. The first two are converted from the reference's World.tscn and World2.tscn ; the reference's third is a copy of the second. Our third joins them into one level wider than the screen. No behaviour of the demo reaches into the engine's insides (R8). Tasks [x] T1 — physics : bodies, gravity, moving one axis at a time in short steps, OnFloor · physics/ · R1, R2 · tests: a falling body lands on the ground and stays there , a fast body does not pass through a thin wall , a body pushed into a wall slides up it , a body on the ground is on the floor [x] T2 — physics : triggers that report when an overlap begins, once · physics/ · R6 · test: touching a trigger is reported once [x] T3 — scene files: bodies, tile maps and sprite sheets with animations, read and written · scenefile/ · R3, R4 · test: a scene with bodies, tiles and animations comes back as written [x] T4 — engine: nodes with bodies stepped every frame, Touched for behaviours · engine/ · R1, R2, R6 · test: a node with a body falls onto a solid node [x] T5 — engine: tile maps drawn in 2D, solid tiles as merged solid bodies · engine/ · R3 · test: solid tiles stop a body , a row of solid tiles is one box [x] T6 — engine: animated sprites, Play , FaceLeft · engine/ · R4 · test: an animation shows each frame for its time and loops [x] T7 — engine: a camera that follows a node within bounds · engine/ · R5 · test: the camera follows its target and stops at the level's edge [x] T8 — engine: RestartScene and ChangeScene , in the window and in the editor's view · engine/ , editor/ · R6, R7 · test: changing scene starts the new one [x] T9 — editor: inspector sections for bodies, sprite sheets and cameras that follow · editor/ · R3–R5 · test: a body set in the inspector is saved [x] T10 — editor: the tile tool (choose, paint, erase) in the 2D view · editor/ · R3 · test: painting a tile and erasing it (and played by hand) [x] T11 — the demo: project, art, Player , Coin , Hazard , Flag , three levels · examples/platformer/ · R1–R8 · played in the editor, in a window and on the 3DS emulator [x] T12 — check on the 3DS: build the demo with TinyGo and play it in the emulator · R7 [x] T13 — the author plays it on the console · R7 (2026-10-18: "funciona en ds") Result Built. In engine : The physics package: boxes that fall, collide and slide, and triggers that report a touch once. Bodies, and tile maps with merged solid rows. Animated sprites that face either way. A camera that follows within bounds. The sky stays open above the tile maps, unless the camera has a ceiling. Restarting or changing scenes. In the editor: inspector sections for bodies, sheets and following cameras, and a tile tool. The demo, in examples/platformer/ , has three forest levels. Two are converted from the reference's Godot levels, and the third joins them. Player , Coin , Hazard and Flag are its only code. Checked. Every requirement's test passes ( go test ./... here and in the demo). A script played the demo in the editor's view, and it was drawn after some seconds. On the 3DS it was built with TinyGo and played in Azahar at 60 frames a second. It walked, jumped over the spikes with A, and restarted on the spikes; the camera rose with the jump. That found a real bug. go-ui hands the scene a fresh copy of its input each frame, so a button was never "pressed". The engine now keeps the game's keys itself ( engine/console.go ). Review. The reviewer's findings were fixed: A node moved or added while playing keeps or gets its body. A body with no size takes short steps. A scene made by hand cannot restart, and says so ( engine.scene-not-restartable ). A missing picture is tried once and costs nothing after. A restart shares the pictures already read ( TakeReplacement , renamed because it acts). Typed frames are checked against the sheet before a run is counted out. Removing an animation forgets the texts typed for the others. The first animation can be unticked. A missing tileset says why. Remove buttons have tooltips. The engine's own code and tests name no coin, spike or player. Not changed, on purpose. DefaultGravity keeps its name: its unit, metres a second each second, is in its comment. Two long editor functions ( followMouse , nodeInspector ) are not split now. Proposal 2's Level task rewrites them instead of splitting them twice. For a person. Play the demo on the console (T13): the jump's height, the camera and the frame rate on the real machine.

proposals/targets-own-screens-and-contro.title: 11. Each target's own screens and controls
proposals/targets-own-screens-and-contro.text: 11. Each target's own screens and controls Status: building · Author's approval: proposal ☑ (2026-10-21, "dale") plan ☑ (2026-10-21, "si") · Controls redesign and R8 ☑ (2026-10-21, "implementalo", "si añade trazos") Why A game made for several devices lays out its interface and reads its controls differently on each, and today it has to do that by hand: pairs of files split by build tags ( controls.go and controls_nintendo3ds.go ); constants such as "has a touch screen"; on the desktop, a picture of the 3DS's touch screen pasted into the middle of the window, with mouse clicks turned into touches. That is one device's layout imposed on another. A game should say what it shows and what the player does, and each target should say where and with which buttons . What Id Requirement Check R1 A game reads actions by name ( Input.Action("menu").Pressed , Input.Action("turn").Value ), with no build tags; engine.json binds each action to inputs per target (keys, mouse buttons, a pad's buttons and sticks, a 3DS's buttons, Android's back) tests of each kind of binding with a made-up input; a sample game with no per-target file R2 The editor shows and edits the bindings, per target capture of the bindings in the editor; a binding changed there reaches the game R3 A game can let the player rebind an action while it plays, and keep it on the device test a binding changed while playing is kept and read back R4 A game paints named surfaces ( "main" , "panel" , "map" …) with go-ui or draw2d, and each target places them: on a 3DS, some on the second screen and touchable; on a computer, in a corner or as a floating window opened and closed, with the mouse as the pointer; on Android, as a bottom sheet captures of one sample on each target; the second screen becomes one way a target places a surface R5 The editor's Play previews each target's layout (today's -3ds view, made general) captures in the editor for each target R6 On a computer and on the web, a game starts windowed or fullscreen as engine.json says per target, and toggles it ( engine.SetFullscreen , engine.Fullscreen() ); a default action (F11, Alt+Enter) does it. On the web it waits for the next click or key, as browsers ask test of the setting; by hand on a desktop and in a browser R8 On a phone the game shows sticks and buttons of its own, designed in the editor (where, how big, named) and bound to actions; with none, the engine's four buttons stay tests of placing and reading them; test a touch control's actions follow its name and go with it R7 What exists keeps working: SetInterface , SetSecondScreen and the keys a game reads today the platformer and lighthouse samples unchanged Out of scope Touch gestures beyond the pointer (swipes, pinches) as actions. A full settings menu for players; the engine gives what one needs (R3), not the menu. Consoles other than the 3DS: the design makes room for them. Design Targets at run time The engine knows which target it runs on (a constant per build: desktop , nintendo3ds , android , web ), named as engine.json names them. project.Target gains Web 's name for the settings, though building for the web stays out of this change. Actions (R1–R3) engine.json gains actions . Each action lists, per target, the inputs that press it, as words a person can read and type: "actions": { "menu": {"desktop": ["Tab", "P", "Pad Start"], "nintendo3ds": ["Start"], "android": ["Back"]}, "fire": {"desktop": ["Space", "Mouse Left", "Pad A"], "nintendo3ds": ["R", "A"]}, "turn": {"desktop": ["A-", "D+", "Left-", "Right+", "Stick X"], "nintendo3ds": ["Circle X", "Left-", "Right+"]} } A button input presses the action: a key, a mouse button, a pad's button, a 3DS's button, Android's back. An axis input moves it from -1 to 1: a stick's axis, or a button with - or + after it. Input.Action(name) gives the action's state this frame: Down , Pressed , Released and its Value (-1 to 1; 1 while a button holds it). One call, one value returned: Go has no overloading, so Input.Down keeps taking keys, which games read today (R7). The bindings are read once into a table of the engine ( engine/actions.go ), so reading an action each frame is a map lookup and some booleans, with nothing allocated. Rebinding (R3): Input.Rebind(action, inputs) changes the current target's inputs, and engine.SaveBindings keeps them in the user's configuration folder (on a 3DS, on the SD card). The game's own engine.json stays as its author wrote it. The editor (R2): a workspace of its own, Controls, designed with the author in a canvas before it was built. The actions are cards on the left, each in a soft colour of its own, with buttons to rename it, switch its kind and remove it, and chips for the controls that do it. The device is drawn in the middle in thin grey lines, as Lucide draws icons, at its real proportions, in tabs: Gamepad, Keyboard and mouse (both kept for desktop and web ), Nintendo 3DS and Mobile ( android ). A control that does an action takes its colour and names it at the drawing's edge with a dotted line. Clicking one opens a panel beside it: a field to find or create an action, and the actions it can do, one chosen (a button presses; a stick's two axes each move one). Every change is saved in engine.json at once, and Ctrl+Z undoes it in this workspace. Strokes (Go Renderer): the drawings' curves need lines, which draw2d did not have. draw2d.Path and List.Stroke draw a path into a smoothed mask kept in the path, shown as a tinted picture, so every backend that draws pictures draws strokes. Touch controls (R8): engine.json's touchControls lists sticks and buttons, each placed and sized as shares of the screen. On Android the game draws them over its view and reads the fingers on them; actions bind them as Touch <name> , and a stick as Touch <name> X and Y . The Mobile tab's Layout designs them: add, drag, resize, rename, remove. Surfaces (R4, R5) engine.SetSurface(name, paint func(context *ui.Context)) names what the game shows. engine.json's surfaces says, per target, where each goes: Place What it is over over the game's view, aligned to an edge or a corner, with a size window a floating window over the view, opened and closed by an action second-screen the second screen (a 3DS's), touchable; several share it in a column sheet a sheet from the bottom (Android), opened and closed by an action none not shown on that target The engine lays each surface out with what Go UI has ( Within , Overlay , PanelWith , Sheet ). SetInterface becomes the surface interface , placed on the second screen on the 3DS and over the view elsewhere, as today (R7). SetSecondScreen 's 3D scene stays as it is. The editor's Play gains a target to preview beside the shapes it has (R5): each target's places for its surfaces. Fullscreen (R6) Go Renderer : input.State.SetFullscreen and Fullscreen , requested like the captured pointer and applied by the window loop with GLFW ( SetMonitor , back to the window's last place and size). The browser loop calls the Fullscreen API on the next key or click. The function keys F1 to F12, and a game pad's buttons, join input.Key and the state. Go UI : a scene's request reaches the window, as its captured pointer does. go-engine : engine.SetFullscreen(bool) and engine.Fullscreen() ; engine.json's window ( windowed or fullscreen ) per target; an action fullscreen , bound to F11 and Alt+Enter on the desktop unless the game binds it otherwise. Alternatives not taken Bindings in code: engine.json lets the editor show them and a player change them without a build. One layout file per target: a table per surface keeps a surface's places side by side. proposals/tools-from-the-editor.title: 5. The tools that build for consoles and phones, set from the editor
proposals/tools-from-the-editor.text: 5. The tools that build for consoles and phones, set from the editor Status: done · Author's approval: proposal ☑ plan ☑ (2026-10-18, "tienes que hacer que se pueda configurar tinygo y android desde ui": approved together) Why Building for the 3DS and Android needs tools found outside the editor: TinyGo, devkitPro, a 3DS emulator, the Android SDK and NDK. Today they are found through environment variables or the usual folders. When they are not, the only way out is a variable set before starting the editor. A person should see what the editor found, and point it at what it did not, in the editor. What Id Requirement Check R1 Where each tool is can be set in the editor, and is kept for every project on this computer (not in the project, which others share) test the tools' places are kept between sessions R2 A place set in the editor comes before the environment and the usual folders; a place set where nothing is says so by its code tests a tool set in the editor is used first , a tool set where nothing is is said by its code R3 The Build workspace shows, for each tool, where it was found or why not, and what it is for capture Out of scope Installing the tools (the panel links to how). The go command itself: the editor runs with one. Design Tools ( internal/build ): a Tools value holds the place of each tool the person chose. It is read from and saved to go-engine/tools.json , in the user's configuration folder ( os.UserConfigDir ). Each finder is a method of it ( tools.FindTinyGo() , tools.FindAndroidSDK() …). It looks in three places, in order: the place chosen, a program or a folder, as the tool is; the variables; the usual folders. project.Open reads it into Project.Tools , so the builds use it. Why it could not be read is kept in Project.ToolsUnread . Panel : under the Build cards, a "Tools on this computer" panel. It has a row per tool: its name, what needs it, a field for its place, and where it was found or the error with its meaning. Check looks where the places typed say. Saving writes the file and looks again, but not while the game builds or plays, since the build reads them. Nothing is looked for every frame. It has a finder for each tool: TinyGo, devkitPro's 3dslink, a 3DS emulator, the Android SDK and its adb, the NDK. A place chosen comes first. A place where the wrong thing is says so with build.tool-place-wrong . That covers nothing there, a folder for a program, a devkitPro with no 3dslink, and an SDK with no adb. Build's Tools on this computer shows each tool, what needs it, and the place typed. It says where the tool was found or why not, with Check and Save. A file that could not be read is said there. Checked. The tests of each requirement pass. The panel was captured with tools found and missing. Then, asked by the author. A file picker, go-ui's own ( ui.FilePicker , feature/3ds 3183ea9, committed with the author's say): Browse beside each tool chooses a program or a folder, as the tool needs. It types it in its field to check and save. Project's Import model chooses a .glb and copies it into assets/models . Nothing in the editor offered that before. For a person. Browse with a real mouse: double clicks, and going through deep folders.

reference/animation.title: animation
reference/animation.text: animation import "github.com/akrck02/go-engine/animation" Package anim moves values over time: a position gliding to a point, a door turning open, a colour fading. A Player runs tweens; each frame the game calls Update with the seconds passed, and every tween writes its value where it was told to. Easing Easing shapes a tween's pace: it takes the share of the time gone (0 to 1) and gives the share of the way gone. type Easing func(share float64) float64 var ( Linear Easing = func(share float64) float64 { return share } EaseIn Easing = func(share float64) float64 { return share * share * share } EaseOut Easing = func(share float64) float64 { rest := 1 - share; return 1 - rest*rest*rest } EaseInOut Easing = func(share float64) float64 { return (1 - math.Cos(share*math.Pi)) / 2 } // Back overshoots the end a little and settles, as something thrown into place. Back Easing = func(share float64) float64 { const overshoot = 1.70158 rest := share - 1 return 1 + (overshoot+1)*rest*rest*rest + overshoot*rest*rest } // Bounce lands like a ball. Bounce Easing = bounce ) Easings. Player Player runs tweens. The zero value is ready. type Player struct { // Has unexported fields. } Function or method func (player *Player) Float(value *float64, target, seconds float64, easing Easing) *Tween Float moves a number to a target in some seconds. func (player *Player) Rotation(value *space.Rotation, target space.Rotation, seconds float64, easing Easing) *Tween Rotation turns a rotation to a target in some seconds, the shorter way round. func (player *Player) Running() int Running is how many tweens are playing or waiting. func (player *Player) StopAll() StopAll stops every tween. func (player *Player) Update(seconds float64) Update moves every tween on by some seconds, and forgets the ones that ended. func (player *Player) Vector(value *space.Vector, target space.Vector, seconds float64, easing Easing) *Tween Vector moves a point (a position, a scale) to a target in some seconds. func (player *Player) Wait(seconds float64) *Tween Wait does nothing for some seconds, then calls what Then gives it: a timer. Tween Tween moves one value from where it is when the tween starts to a target. type Tween struct { // Has unexported fields. } Function or method func (tween *Tween) Delay(seconds float64) *Tween Delay waits some seconds before the tween starts. func (tween *Tween) Done() bool Done tells whether the tween has ended. func (tween *Tween) Loop(times int) *Tween Loop plays the tween again some more times (-1 forever), from the same start. func (tween *Tween) PingPong() *Tween PingPong plays it there and back, forever: a light breathing, a platform going to and fro. func (tween *Tween) Stop() Stop ends the tween where it is, without calling what Then gave it. func (tween *Tween) Then(done func()) *Tween Then calls a function when the tween ends. ← Reference · generated from the doc comments by generate.py

This file holds what the editor does; view.go draws its window with go-ui and viewport.go its 3D view. Functions Function func FieldText(value any) string FieldText writes a field's value for the inspector. func FieldValue(typed string) any FieldValue reads a field as typed in the inspector: a number, true or false, or else text. func Install() Install makes the game open the editor when go-engine starts it to edit it. func ReadFrames(written string, count int) ([]int, error) ReadFrames reads frames written as numbers and runs, separated by commas, of a sheet of a count of frames: "0-3, 6" is 0, 1, 2, 3 and 6. func RunHere() error RunHere opens the editor on the project in the folder the game runs in, with the window's flags from the command line. reference/failure.title: failure
reference/failure.text: failure import "github.com/akrck02/go-engine/failure" Package failure gives every error go-engine returns a code: a stable name, as "engine.scene-not-found", that a program can check and a person can search for. A code is declared once, as a package-level variable, and is itself an error: var SceneNotFound = failure.Define("engine.scene-not-found", "the scene file does not exist") Returning the code alone allocates nothing and comparing it is comparing two pointers, as cheap as Go's own sentinel errors. When the error needs its details (which file, what went wrong underneath), Wrap makes one error with them; that happens while loading or building, never in a game's frame. Callers check an error by its code, wrapped or not: if failure.Is(err, engine.SceneNotFound) { … } errors.Is works the same way, since an error made by Wrap answers to its code. Functions Function func Is(err error, code *Code) bool Is tells whether an error, or any error it wraps, has a code. func Wrap(code *Code, details string, cause error) error Wrap makes an error of a code with its details and the error underneath (nil if none). Code Code is a kind of error: its stable name and what it means. Declare codes with Define. type Code struct { // Has unexported fields. } Function or method func CodeOf(err error) *Code CodeOf is the code of an error, the outermost one that has one; nil for an error without a code (one from outside go-engine). func Define(name, meaning string) *Code Define declares a code. func (code *Code) Error() string Error is the code's name and meaning: a code is an error on its own. func (code *Code) Name() string Name is the code's stable name, as "engine.scene-not-found". Error Error is a coded error with its details: what the code means here, and the error underneath. type Error struct { Code *Code Details string // what is particular to this error: a file, a name Cause error // the error underneath, if any } Function or method func (failed *Error) Error() string Error is the code's name, the details, and the error underneath. func (failed *Error) Is(target error) bool Is tells whether the error has a code: errors.Is(err, code) asks it. func (failed *Error) Unwrap() error Unwrap is the error underneath, so errors.Is and errors.As reach it. ← Reference · generated from the doc comments by generate.py

reference/physics.title: physics
reference/physics.text: physics import "github.com/akrck02/go-engine/physics" Package physics moves boxes in 2D: bodies that fall, collide with solid ground and walls, and slide along them, as a game seen from the side needs. It knows nothing of scenes or nodes; the engine keeps a World in step with them. Bodies are boxes lined up with the axes, in metres, with X to the right and Y up; their Z is not used. A moving body moves one axis at a time, in steps of at most half its smallest side. So even a fast body meets a thin wall instead of jumping over it. Body Body is a box in the world. type Body struct { Kind Kind Position space.Vector // the box's centre, in metres Size space.Vector // the box's width (X) and height (Y), in metres Velocity space.Vector // metres a second GravityScale float64 // how much gravity pulls it: 1 fully, 0 not at all // ZonePull, on a trigger, is the gravity of the area it covers: the falling bodies inside it are // pulled this way instead of the world's (a magnetic field, a room upside down). Nil leaves // the world's. ZonePull *space.Vector // IgnoresZones keeps the world's gravity for the body, inside a zone too: a character that // walks through a field meant for the things it moves. IgnoresZones bool // Has unexported fields. } Function or method func (body *Body) OnFloor() bool OnFloor tells whether the body stood on something solid in the last step. func (body *Body) Pull() space.Vector Pull is the gravity that pulled the body in the last step: the world's, or the zone's it was in. Kind Kind is what a body does in the world. type Kind int const ( // Solid bodies never move: ground, walls, platforms. Moving bodies stop against them. Solid Kind = iota // Moving bodies fall with gravity, move with their velocity and are stopped by solids. Moving // Trigger bodies don't move nor stop anything; they notice the moving and pushable bodies that // touch them (World.Begun). Trigger // Pushable bodies fall and move as moving ones do, and are obstacles to them: a moving body // stands on one, and walking into one pushes it, until a solid stops both (a box, a cart).
