reference/space.title: space
reference/space.text: space import "github.com/akrck02/go-engine/space" Package space is where things are: positions, directions, rotations and sizes in a game's world. Its Transform places a thing: where it is, how it is turned, and how large it is. The world follows glTF and go-renderer. One unit is one metre and Y points up. The axes are right-handed: with X to the right and Y up, Z points towards whoever looks. A camera with no rotation looks along -Z (Forward). Angles are in degrees wherever a person reads or types them. A positive turn is counter-clockwise, looking down the axis towards the origin: a positive turn around Up takes Right (+X) towards Forward (-Z). Functions Function func Degrees(radians float64) float64 Degrees turns radians into degrees. func Radians(degrees float64) float64 Radians turns degrees into radians. Constants and variables const ( Metre = 1.0 Centimetre = 0.01 Kilometre = 1000.0 ) Units: a length of 1 is a metre. var ( Zero = Vector{} One = Vector{1, 1, 1} Right = Vector{1, 0, 0} Up = Vector{0, 1, 0} Back = Vector{0, 0, 1} // towards whoever looks at the world from the front Forward = Vector{0, 0, -1} ) Directions and points that have names. var NoRotation = Rotation{real: 1} NoRotation leaves things as they are. Angles Angles are a rotation as three angles in degrees, the way an inspector shows them: X tilts (pitch), Y turns (yaw) and Z rolls. They apply roll first, then pitch, then yaw, so the yaw is always around the world's vertical, as a character or a camera turns. type Angles struct{ X, Y, Z float64 } Function or method func (angles Angles) Rotation() Rotation Rotation is the rotation the angles describe. Box Box is a box lined up with the axes, from its lowest corner to its highest. type Box struct{ Minimum, Maximum Vector } Function or method func EmptyBox() Box EmptyBox holds nothing; growing it by a point makes a box of that point. func (box Box) Centre() Vector Centre is the box's middle. func (box Box) Contains(point Vector) bool Contains tells whether a point is in the box, its faces included. func (box Box) Corners() [8]Vector Corners are the box's eight corners. func (box Box) Grow(point Vector) Box Grow is the box that holds this one and a point. func (box Box) Hit(origin, direction Vector) (float64, bool) Hit is how far along a ray (from an origin, along a direction of length 1) it first enters the box, if it does. func (box Box) IsEmpty() bool IsEmpty tells whether the box holds nothing. func (box Box) Size() Vector Size is the box's extent along each axis. func (box Box) Transformed(transform Transform) Box Transformed is the box, lined up with the axes again, that holds this box once transformed. func (box Box) Union(other Box) Box Union is the box that holds both. Rotation Rotation is how a thing is turned. Make one with RotationAround, Angles.Rotation or RotationLookingAt; the zero value is not a rotation, NoRotation is. Inside, it is a unit quaternion: a real part and three imaginary ones, which turn vectors without the gimbal lock of angles and blend smoothly from one to another. type Rotation struct { // Has unexported fields. } Function or method func RotationAround(axis Vector, degrees float64) Rotation RotationAround is a turn of some degrees around an axis. func RotationLookingAt(direction, up Vector) Rotation RotationLookingAt is the rotation that makes Forward point along a direction, keeping Up as near the given up as it can. func (rotation Rotation) Angles() Angles Angles are the rotation as angles in degrees, each between -180 and 180 (the pitch between -90 and 90). func (rotation Rotation) Inverse() Rotation Inverse is the rotation that undoes this one. func (rotation Rotation) IsZero() bool IsZero tells whether the rotation is the zero value, which is no rotation at all. func (rotation Rotation) Normalized() Rotation Normalized is the rotation kept to a length of 1, as small errors pile up after many turns. func (rotation Rotation) Parts() (imaginaryX, imaginaryY, imaginaryZ, real float64) Parts are the quaternion's numbers, as go-renderer wants them: the imaginary parts, then the real one. func (rotation Rotation) Rotate(vector Vector) Vector Rotate turns a vector by the rotation. func (rotation Rotation) Then(next Rotation) Rotation Then is the rotation that turns by this one first, then by next. func (rotation Rotation) TurnToward(target Rotation, share float64) Rotation TurnToward is the rotation a share of the way from this one to a target, turning at an even pace the shorter way round: 0 is this rotation, 1 the target. Transform Transform places a thing relative to its parent: it is scaled first, then turned, then moved. type Transform struct { Position Vector Rotation Rotation Scale Vector } Function or method func At(position Vector) Transform At is a transform at a position, unturned, at its own size. func NewTransform() Transform NewTransform is a thing at the origin, unturned, at its own size. func (transform Transform) Angles() Angles Angles are the rotation as angles in degrees. func (transform Transform) DirectionToParent(local Vector) Vector DirectionToParent is where a direction in the thing's own space points in its parent's (turned, not scaled). func (transform Transform) Forward() Vector Forward is the way the thing faces, in its parent's space. func (transform Transform) FromParent(point Vector) Vector FromParent is where a point given in the parent's space is in the thing's own space: ToParent undone. func (transform *Transform) LookAt(target Vector) LookAt turns the thing so its Forward points at a target, keeping its Up towards the sky. func (transform Transform) Matrix() graphics.Mat4 Matrix is the transform as go-renderer draws it. func (transform *Transform) Move(offset Vector) Move moves the thing by an offset in its parent's space. func (transform Transform) Place(child Transform) Transform Place is where a child is, placed by its own transform inside the thing this transform places: the child's transform in the thing's parent's space. func (transform Transform) Right() Vector Right is the thing's right, in its parent's space. func (transform *Transform) SetAngles(angles Angles) SetAngles sets the rotation from angles in degrees. func (transform Transform) ToParent(local Vector) Vector ToParent is where a point given in the thing's own space is in its parent's space. func (transform *Transform) Turn(axis Vector, degrees float64) Turn turns the thing around an axis of its parent's space by some degrees. func (transform Transform) Up() Vector Up is the thing's up, in its parent's space. Vector Vector is a point or a direction in the world, in metres. type Vector struct{ X, Y, Z float64 } Function or method func NewVector(x, y, z float64) Vector NewVector makes a vector from its three coordinates. func (vector Vector) Add(other Vector) Vector Add is the vector moved by another. func (vector Vector) Cross(other Vector) Vector Cross is the cross product: a direction square to both, by the right-hand rule. func (vector Vector) Distance(other Vector) float64 Distance is how far apart two points are. func (vector Vector) Dot(other Vector) float64 Dot is the dot product: how much two directions point the same way, times their lengths. func (vector Vector) Length() float64 Length is how long the vector is. func (vector Vector) MultiplyEach(other Vector) Vector MultiplyEach multiplies each axis by the other vector's: a size scaled per axis. func (vector Vector) Near(other Vector, tolerance float64) bool Near tells whether two vectors are the same within a tolerance on each axis. func (vector Vector) Normalized() Vector Normalized is the vector's direction with a length of 1 (Zero stays Zero). func (vector Vector) Scale(factor float64) Vector Scale is the vector times a number. func (vector Vector) Subtract(other Vector) Vector Subtract is the vector from other to this one. func (vector Vector) Toward(other Vector, share float64) Vector Toward is the point a share of the way from this one to another: 0 is this point, 1 the other. ← Reference · generated from the doc comments by generate.py

the-quest/a-forest-of-your-own.title: 🧭 Level 1: a forest of your own
the-quest/a-forest-of-your-own.text: 🧭 Level 1: a forest of your own You make the game's project, a 2D scene, and the forest behind everything: hills, trees and a sky. At the end you can play it, even though nothing moves yet. The idea A 2D scene is a stage seen from the front. Its pictures are flat cut-outs standing at different depths: the hills at the back, the trees in front of them, later the slime in front of all. The camera is the window the player looks through. The project go-engine new ~/games/forest "Forest" The editor opens on a 3D scene with a cube. This game is 2D, so it needs pictures. Take the forest's from the engine's own example: git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/akrck02/go-engine.git /tmp/go-engine cp -r /tmp/go-engine/examples/platformer/assets/sprites ~/games/forest/assets/ In Project (key 1) the folder sprites appears, with the pictures: the forest's tiles, its backdrops, a slime, a coin, spikes and a sign. A 2D scene Click the scene's name at the top ( main ) and choose New 2D scene . It opens with a green ground, a square and a camera. Choose the Square in the tree on the left and delete it with the bin above the tree. Click an empty part of the view to choose nothing: the inspector shows the Scene . Name it Forest , make the sky #11adc1 , and set Pixels per metre to 16. The forest's tiles are 16 pixels across, so each tile will be a metre. The backdrop In Project , open sprites and choose background-far.png . Press Place in the scene . The editor goes back to Level , where the picture is a node named after it. Rename it Hills , and set its Draw order to 0.1. Do the same with background-near.png : name it Trees , draw order 0.2. A greater draw order is drawn in front. Drag both so they sit together behind the ground. The camera Choose the Camera . Its inspector says how many metres it sees: set Metres seen, top to bottom to 9.4 and across to 15.5. Drag it over the hills; the white frame is what the player will see. Last, tell the game to start here. In Project , press Settings and choose this scene as The scene the game starts with . Save with Ctrl+S. Checkpoint Press Play (key 5). You see the hills, the trees and the green ground through the camera. Press 3DS above the view to see it at the console's shape. Bonus: a dusk sky Make the sky the deep blue of a late evening. Achievement unlocked: Explorer You made a project, a 2D scene and a camera. ← The quest · Level 2 →

the-quest/a-slime-that-walks.title: 🎭 Level 2: a slime that walks
the-quest/a-slime-that-walks.text: 🎭 Level 2: a slime that walks You bring in the hero, a slime, give it a body that falls and stands, and write your first behaviour: the code that walks and jumps when the player presses the arrows and Space. The idea The slime is two nodes, as a puppet is a body and a costume. Player is the body: the physics moves it, and your code tells it where to go. Its child Sprite is the costume: the picture that follows the body and plays its animations. Keeping them apart lets the costume sit a little higher than the body, or change, without the physics noticing. The slime's animations Open the forest project of level 1. In Project , choose slime.sprite.json (it came with the pictures you copied) and press Open in Art . A sprite file cuts a picture into frames, here 5 across and 2 down, and names runs of them: idle is frame 0, walk frames 0 to 3 at 3 a second, looping. The other frames are spare. Choose an animation to watch it under Preview ; Play it when the scene starts would make it the one the slime starts with. To make one of your own, choose any picture in Project and press Make it a sprite or a tileset . Something to stand on Back in Level , choose the Ground , the green box the new scene came with (a flat shape: a cube is drawn as a square in 2D). In its inspector, under Body , press Give it a body . Leave it Solid : it never moves, and what falls lands on it. The body Press + above the tree and choose Empty . Name the new node Player . Give it a body, and choose Moving . Under the kinds, set its size: width 0.94, height 0.63 metres, the slime's own shape. Set its gravity scale to 5.75: it falls with 5.75 times Earth's pull. Games make their heroes fall much faster than real things do; it feels better under the thumbs. An empty node shows only as a small dot: set its position in the inspector, X 8 and Y 0, above the ground. The costume With Player chosen, go to Project , choose slime.sprite.json and press Place in the scene . A new node lands after Player , and is chosen. Over the tree, press Make it a child of the node above (the third arrow; its tooltip says so). Name it Sprite . A child's position is from its parent, and both are centred on their position. The slime's picture is a little taller than its body, so set the sprite's Y to 0.19: its feet then sit on the body's bottom. The code Add a file player.go beside main.go : package main import "github.com/akrck02/go-engine/engine" // Player walks with the arrows (or the 3DS's cross), jumps with Space (or A) while it stands on // the ground, and plays its sprite's animations. type Player struct { Speed float64 `json:"speed"` // metres a second, walking Jump float64 `json:"jump"` // metres a second, upwards, when it jumps } // Update runs every frame. func (player *Player) Update(context *engine.Context) { body, found := context.Node.Body() if !found { return } direction := context.Input.Move().X body.Velocity.X = direction * player.Speed if context.Input.Pressed(engine.KeySpace) && body.OnFloor() { body.Velocity.Y = player.Jump } player.animate(context.Node, direction) } // animate plays "walk" while the player walks and "idle" while it stands, facing the way it goes. func (player *Player) animate(node *engine.Node, direction float64) { sprite, found := node.Find("Sprite") if !found { return } if direction == 0 { sprite.Play("idle") return } sprite.Play("walk") sprite.FaceLeft(direction > 0) // the slime is drawn facing left } The code never moves the slime itself. It sets the body's velocity , how fast it goes, and the physics moves it, stopping it at the ground. Move() is -1, 0 or 1 across, from the arrows, the 3DS's cross or a phone's buttons. Space is also the 3DS's A. OnFloor() keeps the slime from jumping in the air. node.Find("Sprite") finds the child named Sprite , and found says whether it is there. The slime's picture faces left: FaceLeft(true) mirrors it, so walking right ( direction > 0 ) shows it facing right. Then register it in main.go , whose line engine.Register(Spin{}) becomes: engine.Register(Spin{}, Player{}) In Code (key 4), press Rebuild . It saves the scene, builds the game again, and reopens the editor where you were. The behaviour Choose Player . Under Behaviours , press Add and choose Player . Its fields appear: set speed to 3.2 and jump to 18.75. Checkpoint Press Play . The slime falls onto the ground; the arrows walk it, Space jumps. The slime should turn the way it walks, and wobble while it walks. If it does not move, check in Code that Player is listed: the scene names the behaviour by its Go type's name. If it falls through the ground, check that the ground's body is Solid ; Bodies , over the view, outlines every body. Bonus: run Make the slime run twice as fast while Shift, or X (the keyboard's, or the 3DS's button), is held. Achievement unlocked: Puppeteer You gave a node a body and moved it with your own code. ← Level 1 · Level 3 →

the-quest/coins-and-water.title: 🪙 Level 4: coins and water
the-quest/coins-and-water.text: 🪙 Level 4: coins and water A level needs something to win and something to lose. You add coins that vanish when touched, water that sends the slime back to the start, and a sign that ends the level. The idea A trigger is a body that stops nothing: an invisible tripwire. When a moving body walks into it, the engine calls the trigger's behaviours with Touched , and tells them what touched. A coin, a pool of water and a finishing sign are the same thing with different code. The code Three small behaviours, each in its own file beside main.go . coin.go : package main import "github.com/akrck02/go-engine/engine" // Coin is collected when the player touches it. type Coin struct{} // Touched runs when a moving body begins touching the coin. func (coin *Coin) Touched(context *engine.Context, other *engine.Node) { player, found := engine.Behaviour[Player](other) if !found { return } player.Coins++ context.Node.Remove() } engine.Behaviour[Player](other) finds the Player behaviour on what touched, so only the slime collects coins. Give Player somewhere to count them, a field the scene does not set: Coins int `json:"-"` // the coins collected: not a setting hazard.go starts the level again, and flag.go goes to another scene: // Hazard starts the level again when the player touches it: spikes, water. type Hazard struct{} func (hazard *Hazard) Touched(context *engine.Context, other *engine.Node) { if _, isPlayer := engine.Behaviour[Player](other); isPlayer { context.RestartScene() } } // Flag ends the level when the player touches it, and goes on to the next one. type Flag struct { Next string `json:"next"` // the next level's scene file, as "scenes/forest-2.scene.json" } func (flag *Flag) Touched(context *engine.Context, other *engine.Node) { if _, isPlayer := engine.Behaviour[Player](other); isPlayer { context.ChangeScene(flag.Next) } } Each file starts with package main and imports engine , as player.go does. Register them in main.go , engine.Register(Spin{}, Player{}, Coin{}, Hazard{}, Flag{}) , and press Rebuild . Code then lists them, with where each is used: Coins In Project , place coin.sprite.json . It spins: the sprite file starts its spin animation by itself. Give it a body, Trigger , 1 by 1 metres. Add the behaviour Coin . Drag it over a ledge. Press Duplicate (Ctrl+D) for more, and drag each where a jump reaches. Water Under the ledges, the slime falls forever. Catch it: Press + , Empty , and name it Water . Drag it under the level. Give it a body, Trigger , 30 metres wide and 4 high. Add the behaviour Hazard . It is invisible, and needs not be seen: falling off is the danger. Bodies over the view draws triggers in orange. The sign Place sign.png at the level's far end. Give it a body, Trigger , 1 by 2 metres. Add the behaviour Flag , and set next to scenes/scene-2.scene.json : this same level, for now. The bonus makes a second one. Checkpoint Press Play . Collect the coins, fall into the water, start again, and reach the sign. In Play , choose Player in the list on the left: Watch shows where it is and how it moves, frame by frame. Pause and Step stop the game and move it one frame at a time. Bonus: a second level Make a second level, and send the sign there. Achievement unlocked: Collector Your level can be won and lost. ← Level 3 · Level 5 →

the-quest/ground-to-stand-on.title: 🧱 Level 3: ground to stand on
the-quest/ground-to-stand-on.text: 🧱 Level 3: ground to stand on The green box was a stand-in. Now you paint a real level with the forest's tiles, ledges to jump between, and make the camera follow the slime through it. The idea A tile map is a grid, like squared paper, and a tileset is a box of stamps: small square pictures of grass, rock and earth. Painting the level is stamping tiles into squares. Some stamps are solid : the physics turns each row of solid tiles into ground, so you never draw a body for the floor by hand. The tileset In Project , choose forest.tileset.json and press Open in Art . It cuts the forest's picture into tiles of 16 pixels. The tiles tinted blue are solid: grass on top, rock and earth below. Click a tile on the picture to make bodies stand on it; click it again to let them through. The map In Level , delete the green box, Ground : the tiles will be the ground now. Press + and choose Tile map . Name it Ground . In its inspector, choose the tileset assets/sprites/forest.tileset.json . Set the cells: 14 across, 8 down. The map's top-left corner is the node's position. Keep the slime above where you will paint. Painting The palette under the view shows the tileset. Choose a tile in it, then a tool on the left of the view: Tool Key What it does Paint B Stamps the tile where you click or drag Erase E Empties the cells you click or drag Fill G Fills the empty cells joined to the one you click Select V Back to choosing and dragging nodes Paint a long ledge for the slime to start on, then two or three smaller ones, each a jump away. Bodies , over the view, fills the solid tiles in blue: that is where the slime will stand. A camera that follows Choose the Camera . Under Follows , choose Player , and set the smoothing to 0.2 seconds: the camera catches up gently instead of jerking. Leave Its view keeps inside on The tile maps , so the player never sees past the level's edges. Checkpoint Press Play and run from ledge to ledge. The camera follows the slime, and stops where the tiles end. If the slime falls through a ledge, check in Art that its tiles are solid. Bonus: a gap that matters Leave a gap two tiles wide between two ledges, and make the slime need a run-up to cross it. Achievement unlocked: Builder You painted a level and made the camera follow your hero. ← Level 2 · Level 4 →

the-quest/in-your-pocket.title: 🎒 Level 6: in your pocket
the-quest/in-your-pocket.text: 🎒 Level 6: in your pocket Your forest is a game. Now it leaves the editor: a program for your computer, a .3dsx for a Nintendo 3DS, and an .apk for an Android phone. Then a final challenge. The idea The same Go code becomes three programs. For a computer, Go builds it as it is. For the 3DS, TinyGo for the 3DS builds it for the console's processor, and devkitPro packs it for the Homebrew Launcher. For Android, the phone's tools wrap it in an app. The editor runs each of them for you, from Build (key 6). On your computer In Build , the card This computer has Build : it writes the game into build/ , without the editor inside, with the notices of the code it carries beside it. Play opens it in a window of its own. Send that folder to a friend on the same system, and they can play. On a Nintendo 3DS The 3DS needs two tools. Open the Tools tab: Beside TinyGo , press Install . It downloads TinyGo for the 3DS's latest release and remembers where it put it. Beside devkitPro , press Install . Its own installer opens in a terminal and asks for your password: it installs 3ds-dev . For an emulator, press Install beside 3DS emulator : it fetches Azahar. Back in Platforms , the Nintendo 3DS card's Build writes build/forest.3dsx . Emulator opens it in Azahar: On a real console with the Homebrew Launcher, open the Launcher and press Y, then press Send : the game travels over Wi-Fi and starts. The cross walks, A jumps. On an Android phone In Tools , install the Android SDK , which brings the Android NDK with it (you read and accept its licence first), and a JDK if the computer has none. Plug a phone in with USB debugging on, or start an emulator, then press Play on device on the Android card. The game shows round buttons to walk and jump, and its log streams into the editor while it runs. Checkpoint Your game runs somewhere other than the editor. On the 3DS it holds 60 frames a second, lights and all. 🏆 Final challenge: a lift The level's far end gets a cliff too high to jump. Build a lift: a ledge that rises and sinks, and carries the slime up. Hints: a body of the kind Platform moves at the velocity its behaviours give it, and carries what stands on it. A behaviour can remember where its node started in Start . Achievement unlocked: Lift engineer Achievement unlocked: Traveller Your game runs on a computer, a console and a phone. You finished the quest. 🎉 The guides go further into each part, and the complete game has three levels to compare with yours. ← Level 5 · The guides →

the-quest/night-in-the-forest.title: 🏮 Level 5: night in the forest
the-quest/night-in-the-forest.text: 🏮 Level 5: night in the forest Night falls on the forest. You darken it with an ambient light, hang a lamp over the sign, make the coins glow and let a cold moonlight in. No code, except for the bonus. The idea Think of the level as a stage. The ambient is the house lights: how much of everything you can see when nothing else shines. Each light is a spotlight: it adds its colour where it reaches, strongest in its middle and fading at its edge. A sprite light is a light in the shape of a picture: a coin that glows exactly where its gold is. Dusk Choose nothing (click an empty part of the view). In the scene's inspector, tick An ambient light of its own . Make it a dark blue, #30406e , at an intensity of 0.55. The forest dims at once: the view shows the scene lit as the game will be. Lit , over the view, switches that on and off while you work. A lamp over the sign Choose the Sign . Press + and choose Light : a warm lamp lands after it. Press Make it a child of the node above (↳), so the lamp moves with the sign. Name it Lamp and set its Y to 1.4, just above the board. In its Light section, keep Point . Set the intensity to 1.5, Inner to 0.5 metres and Outer to 4. Lights , over the view, draws two circles round it: where its light is full, and where it ends. Coins that glow Choose a coin, and from Project place coin.sprite.json again. Make it a child of the coin (↳) and name it Glow . Under Light , press Make it a light and choose Sprite . Make it #ffe08a , at 1.2. A sprite light is not drawn itself: it shines in its picture's shape, so the coin seems to glow from inside. Do the same for each coin, or glow one and duplicate the coin. Moonlight Press + , Light , and drag it high over the far end of the level. Make it a pale blue, #9ab8ff , at 0.8, with an inner radius of 1 and an outer of 7. Checkpoint Press Play and run through the dark. The lamp warms the sign and its ledge, the coins glow, and the far end is blue under the moon. The light the lamp throws on the sky beyond the hills is part of the scene too: everything drawn is lit. Bonus: a lamp that flickers Make the lamp waver, as a flame does. Achievement unlocked: Lamplighter You lit a scene with an ambient, lamps and glows. ← Level 4 · Level 6 →

the-quest/the-quest.title: 🗺️ The quest: a forest platformer
the-quest/the-quest.text: 🗺️ The quest: a forest platformer The quest's map: from the start, Explorer, Puppeteer, Builder, Collector, Lamplighter and Traveller, then the final challenge, Lift engineer In six levels you make one game, a step at a time. A slime walks and jumps through a forest. It collects coins, avoids the water and reaches a sign at the end, at night, under lamps. Then you play it on a Nintendo 3DS. Each level adds a little to the game before it, and ends with something you can play. Before you start , follow Get started : Go Engine installed and a first project played. Each level takes fifteen to twenty minutes. Every level has the same shape: the idea , in everyday words; the steps , in the editor and in code; a checkpoint , to know it works; a bonus , with its solution folded; an achievement to unlock. Level You learn You end with Achievement 1. A forest of your own 2D scenes, pictures, the camera A forest you can look at 🧭 Explorer 2. A slime that walks Sprites, bodies, your first behaviour A slime you move with the arrows 🎭 Puppeteer 3. Ground to stand on Tile maps, solid tiles, a camera that follows A level to run and jump through 🧱 Builder 4. Coins and water Triggers, Touched , changing scenes A level you can win and lose 🪙 Collector 5. Night in the forest The ambient, point lights, sprite lights The forest at night, lit by lamps 🏮 Lamplighter 6. In your pocket Building for a computer, the 3DS and Android Your game on a console 🎒 Traveller A final challenge waits at the end of level 6: a lift that carries the slime up a cliff. These are the achievements to collect on the way: The seven achievements: Explorer, Puppeteer, Builder, Collector, Lamplighter, Traveller and Lift engineer 💡 The pictures come from godot-generic-platformer , under the MIT licence. The finished game is in examples/platformer . Look there whenever you are lost. ← Core ideas · Level 1 →

troubleshooting.title: 🩹 Troubleshooting
troubleshooting.text: 🩹 Troubleshooting The problems people meet, and their fixes. Every error Go Engine reports has a code , as engine.scene-not-found : search this page for it. Common problems go install fails with "cgo" or "gcc". The editor's window needs a C compiler and OpenGL's headers. On Debian or Ubuntu: sudo apt install gcc libgl1-mesa-dev xorg-dev libwayland-dev libxkbcommon-dev . On macOS: xcode-select --install . The editor opens, but a behaviour is "Not in the project's code (yet?)". The editor runs inside your game, so new code needs Rebuild (in Code). If it still shows, the behaviour is not registered: add it to engine.Register(…) in main.go . A behaviour's field does not change anything. The scene fills exported fields by their JSON name: check the tag, as `json:"speed"` , and that the field starts with a capital letter. The player falls through the ground. Its body must be Moving and the ground's Solid , or the tiles must be solid in the tileset (in Art , tinted blue). Bodies , over the view, shows both. A node moves in the editor but jumps back when played. Move bodies by their velocity, never by their transform, while the game plays. Lights do nothing. In 2D, check Lit over the view is on. A light reaches only its outer radius: Lights draws it. On the 3DS, a 3D lamp lights a floor only where it has vertices. The 3DS build fails. Build → Tools checks each tool: TinyGo must be TinyGo for the 3DS (its own TinyGo has no nintendo3ds target), and devkitPro needs its 3ds-dev packages. Send finds no console. Open the Homebrew Launcher and press Y before Send . If the network hides the console, set its address in Project → Settings . Every error code Code What happened, and what to do build.3dslink-not-found sending to the 3DS needs devkitPro's 3dslink (the 3ds-dev package): install it or set its folder in Build's tools, or $DEVKITPRO build.adb-not-found playing on an Android device needs adb, the SDK's platform-tools build.android-ndk-incomplete the Android NDK has no compilers for this system: install another version of it build.android-ndk-not-found building for Android needs the Android NDK, in the SDK's ndk folder (Android Studio's SDK Manager): install it or set its place in Build's tools, or $ANDROID_NDK_HOME build.android-sdk-incomplete the Android SDK lacks parts a build needs: install them with its SDK Manager, or Install build.android-sdk-not-found building for Android needs the Android SDK (Android Studio installs it): install it or set its place in Build's tools, or $ANDROID_HOME build.devkitpro-incomplete devkitPro lacks parts of the 3DS's: install its 3ds-dev packages (Install runs devkitPro's installer) build.java-not-found Android's builds need a JDK (17 or newer, as Adoptium's Temurin, or Android Studio's): install one or set its folder in Build's tools, or $JAVA_HOME build.java-without-compiler the Java found is only a runtime, with no javac: Android's builds need a JDK build.nintendo3ds-emulator-not-found no 3DS emulator found (azahar, lime3ds, citra-qt or
